title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Recap and Roadmap
Last time: Dedekind & Cantor’s existential, set-theoretic style of mathematics — and Russell’s paradox, which broke Frege’s comprehension principle.
Today

paradoxes and consistency, predicativity, the axiom of choice
Brouwer’s intuitionism vs. Hilbert’s program

The question throughout: what is a legitimate mathematical object, definition, or proof?

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Comprehension Principle, Again
Recall the principle that broke under Russell’s paradox:
\[
\text{for any well-defined property } p,\ \text{there exists } \{x : p(x)\}
\]

This was the basis for the logicist understanding of set theory — “naive” set theory
Not just Russell’s paradox: two families of paradoxes emerged around 1900

set-theoretic paradoxes (Burali-Forti, Cantor, Russell/Zermelo)
semantic paradoxes (Richard, König, Grelling) — about truth and definability

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Set-Theoretic Paradoxes

Burali-Forti (1897; Cantor 1896): the set of all ordinals would itself be well-ordered, hence have an ordinal \(>\) every ordinal in it — contradiction
Cantor (1899): the set of all cardinals leads to the same kind of contradiction
Zermelo–Russell (1901–02): let \(p(x)\) be “\(x \notin x\)” and consider \(R = \{x : x \notin x\}\)

Comprehension is contradictory in the simplest possible way — no need for a theory of the transfinite to state it.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Hilbert and Existence
Hilbert abandoned logicism. He proposed working with axiom systems that comprise non-logical axioms.
This, however, requires a new kind of justification why the ojects we are trying to axiomatize exist.
Hilbert’s proposal:

A set of objects “exists” only if we can prove its defining axiom system consistent
concept \(\to\) set becomes consistency proof \(\to\) legitimate existence
Objects have a kind of ideal existence “in the realm of thought,” not independent metaphysical existence

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Predicativity — Poincaré’s Diagnosis
When Frege’s and Russell’s paradoxes became widely known (1903), Poincaré offered his own culprit: impredicative definitions.

A definition is impredicative when it refers to a totality that already contains the very element being defined.


Example: least upper bound – defining the supremum involves quantifying over “all upper bounds,” a set of real numbers, in order to pin down a particular real number. That real number is thus specified by reference to a totality it belongs to.
Poincaré: this kind of circularity is exactly what licenses the paradoxes

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Richard’s Paradox (a Semantic Paradox)

Only countably many reals are definable by a finite expression — list them \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots\) (lexicographic order)
Define \(r\): the \(n\)th decimal digit of \(r\) differs from the \(n\)th digit of \(a_n\)
\(r\) is not on the list — yet \(r\) was just defined, in finitely many words!

Poincaré’s diagnosis: \(r\)’s definition refers to the totality of all definable numbers, of which \(r\) is itself meant to be a member. Impredicative.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Two Responses to Impredicativity


Zermelo — unconvinced

Impredicative definitions are everywhere in classical analysis (e.g. least upper bound)
Harmless: the object isn’t created by the definition, only singled out from what already exists


Russell — convinced

Adopts Poincaré’s “vicious circle principle”
Builds a theory of types: objects stratified into levels; no set of “mixed” type
Result: Principia Mathematica (1910–13)

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Where Predicativity Led

Russell’s ramified type theory needed extra ad hoc machinery (the axiom of reducibility) to recover ordinary mathematics
Weyl, in Das Kontinuum (1918), tried a leaner predicative foundation: accept classical logic and \(\mathbb{N}\), but build the reals predicatively

cost: \(\mathbb{R}\) is no longer complete — the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem fails

Predicative mathematics survives today as a serious middle ground between classical and constructive mathematics

title: The Foundational Crisis
section: Controversy on the Axiom of Choice
text:
Controversy on the Axiom of Choice
Zermelo (1904): \(\mathrm{AC} \implies\) every set — in particular \(\mathbb{R}\) — can be well-ordered.

\(\mathrm{AC}\): given any family of disjoint nonempty sets, a choice set exists containing one element from each
The proof gives no explicit construction of the well-ordering
Critics: \(\mathrm{AC}\) merely asserts the choice set exists, without a defining property for it

\(\Rightarrow\) a deep debate followed, cutting across the logicism/predicativism divide.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
From Controversy to Axiom System
The AC debate spurred Zermelo to work out his axiom system for set theory (1908) — a careful, mathematical (not logical) analysis of Cantor’s and Dedekind’s set theory.

Fraenkel & von Neumann (1920s) add: Replacement and Regularity
Weyl & Skolem: formalize within first-order logic — quantify only over sets, not over properties

\[
\rightsquigarrow \quad \mathrm{ZF(C)}
\]

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
What ZFC Codifies
ZFC settles the early-1900s controversies by simply building in the modern, anti-Kroneckerian traits:

impredicative definitions — allowed
arbitrary functions and subsets — allowed
purely existential proofs — allowed


The result: a working “Platonistic” view of mathematics — the objects a theory refers to are treated as if they exist independently of what a mathematician can explicitly define or construct.

By the 1920s, Russell’s (simplified) type theory and Zermelo’s set theory had largely converged on this same methodology.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Summary - Response to the Paradoxes
The paradoxes did not kill modern mathematics.

They forced a clarification: existence via consistency, not naive comprehension
Poincaré’s predicativism and Russell’s type theory tried to restrain the new methods
Zermelo’s set theory — soon ZFC — codified the new methods instead.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
A New Kind of Critique
1921: Weyl publishes a paper in the Mathematische Zeitschrift — a disciple of Hilbert’s — openly siding with Brouwer, diagnosing a “crisis in the foundations.”

Weyl’s paper: deliberately a propaganda pamphlet, “to rouse the sleepers”
Hilbert’s reply, same year: Brouwer and Weyl are attempting a “putsch” — a “dictatorship à la Kronecker”

The foundational debate turns into open battle: Hilbert’s classical mathematics vs. Brouwer’s constructive “revolution.”

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
What is Brouwer’s “Revolution”?
Up to 1920, the debate concerned: real numbers, impredicativity, and the strong existential assumptions of set theory (esp. AC).
Brouwer went further: 

He put classical logic itself on trial: quantifiers over infinite domains, and the principle of excluded middle (PEM)
Poincaré, Klein, and others had said logic is not the whole of mathematics; Brouwer said mathematics is prior to and independent of logic and language altogether.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Intuitionism — First Principles

For Brouwer, mathematical objects are mental constructions; mathematics does not depend on language or logic to exist
Classical logic (including PEM) was abstracted from experience with finite sets — and wrongly extrapolated to infinite ones
PEM: \(p \vee \neg p\) — “either \(p\) or not \(p\)” — always holds, classically

Brouwer’s claim: this is not a law of thought, but an unjustified generalization.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Constructive Standard

Consequence: proof by contradiction is invalid.

Classically: assume \(\neg p\), derive a contradiction, conclude \(p\)
Constructively: this only shows \(\neg\neg p\) — not the same as a construction of \(p\)

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
A Different Notion of Truth
For a constructivist:

“\(p\) is true” means: we possess a proof of \(p\) by stringent constructive methods
“\(p\) is false” means: we possess a counterexample to \(p\)


To a constructivist, the statement “π is normal” currently has no truth value — not true, not false, not “unknown-but-determinate.” Truth is not timeless; it is made.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Rebuilding Analysis: Choice Sequences
Brouwer (1918) replaces Cantorian sets with constructive substitutes: spreads and species.

A choice sequence: a sequence of rationals not required to be fully specified in advance

may be generated by a fixed rule (e.g. Newton’s method for \(\sqrt 2\))
or by choices the mathematician makes freely, over time, subject to constraints


Intuitionistic mathematics is “mathematics in the making” — unlike the timeless, fully-determinate objects of classical analysis.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Spreads and a New Continuum

A spread is a law regulating which choice sequences are admissible — the basis for Brouwer’s reconstruction of \(\mathbb{R}\)
The continuum becomes a genuinely continuous domain, not a set of pre-existing points

an echo of Aristotle: the continuum is not made up of unextended points


A function on a spread must be determined from a finite initial segment of any choice sequence — this has a startling consequence.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Startling Consequence
Every intuitionistically total function on \(\mathbb{R}\) is (uniformly) continuous.

The classical step function \[
f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \leq 0 \\ 1 & x > 0 \end{cases}
\] is not a legitimate function for Brouwer
Reason: deciding \(x > 0\) vs. \(x \leq 0\) is not always possible — not decidable from a finite stage of the sequence

(Anticipates the later, independent discovery that all computable real functions are continuous — Turing and others.)

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Cost of Intuitionism
Rebuilding analysis this way is hard. Weyl, who once championed Brouwer’s program, wrote in 1925:

“The mathematician watches with pain the largest part of his towering theories dissolve into mist before his eyes.”

Brouwer himself, unfazed, replied (1933):

“The spheres of truth are less transparent than those of illusion.”

Weyl abandoned intuitionism shortly after. But Hilbert had another answer in mind.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Hilbert’s Program
Hilbert (1928): to “eliminate from the world once and for all the skeptical doubts” about classical mathematics.

Strategy: use Kroneckerian (finitary, constructive) means to justify anti-Kroneckerian (classical) methods
Key move: turn proofs into formal, syntactic objects — finite strings of symbols manipulated by explicit rules
A proof becomes something a finitary, combinatorial argument can reason about, from the outside — metamathematics

title: The Foundational Crisis
section: The Four Steps of the Program
text:
The Four Steps of the Program

Find suitable axioms and primitive concepts for a theory \(T\) (e.g. the real numbers)
Find axioms and rules for classical logic — syntactic rules turning propositions into new propositions
Formalize \(T\): propositions become strings of symbols, proofs become sequences of strings obeying formal rules
Give a finitary proof that no string expressing a contradiction can ever be the last line of a proof

If (iv) succeeds for \(T\): consistency is established by means even a strict finitist should accept.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Finitism: What Counts as “Given”
Hilbert’s answer to Poincaré’s 1905 circularity worry (a consistency proof for arithmetic would need induction):

What is genuinely, intuitively given: signs and formulas themselves, as concrete finite objects
Metamathematical reasoning about them needs only a very weak form of induction — much weaker than full arithmetical induction
Finitary mathematics needs no further justification — it is where justification bottoms out

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Progress and Limits (1920s)

Propositional logic: proved consistent and complete
First-order (predicate) logic: proved complete — Gödel’s dissertation, 1929
Ackermann, von Neumann: consistency results for subsystems of arithmetic (1928–1930)
By 1930 Hilbert believed full consistency of arithmetic was within reach

A crucial hidden assumption: that the axiomatic systems in question would also be complete.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
“Formalism” — a Slightly Misleading Name

The label comes from Hilbert’s method: formalize a theory, study its formal proof-structure
But Hilbert did not think mathematics is a meaningless game with symbols

he consistently stressed the meaningfulness of informal mathematical statements

Unlike intuitionism, formalism was never a full philosophy of mathematics — it was a method for justifying the classical one

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
A Personal Crisis, Too
The dispute was not only intellectual.

Hilbert and Brouwer: strong-willed, brilliant, and deeply incompatible personalities
1928: Hilbert moves to remove Brouwer from the editorial board of Mathematische Annalen

Einstein: the move is “unwise” and wants no part of it
The board is dissolved and reconstituted without Brouwer — the journal loses Einstein and Carathéodory

Brouwer, disturbed, withdraws from the scene for years — as political tensions fade, so does the sense of “crisis”

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Looking Ahead
 
Hilbert’s program looked to be within reach by 1930 — one more push on the consistency of arithmetic.
 
Things turned out otherwise…

title: Relations and Functions
text: You have used relations (orderings) and functions all your life; the point here is to say what they are inside axiomatic set theory, and to notice where an extra axiom (Replacement) is needed to build them.

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Relations
Definition (binary relation). \(R\) is a (binary) relation iff \(R\) is a set of ordered pairs:
\[
\forall u \in R\;\exists x, y\;\bigl(u = \langle x, y\rangle\bigr).
\]
Here \(\forall u \in R\,(\dots)\) is shorthand for \(\forall u\,(u \in R
\rightarrow \dots)\). We write
\[
x \mathbin{R} y \quad\text{for}\quad \langle x, y\rangle \in R,
\qquad\qquad
x \mathbin{\not\mathrel{R}} y \quad\text{for}\quad \langle x, y\rangle \notin R.
\]
The abbreviations \(x \mathbin{R} y\) and \(x \mathbin{\not\mathrel{R}} y\) are meaningful even when \(R\) is not a relation — we will use this later.

Usual terminology
Fix a set \(A\). The following say what it means for \(R\) to have a property on \(A\); each is just an abbreviation, obtained by plugging \(R\) into a formula.

transitive: \(x \mathbin{R} y \wedge y \mathbin{R} z \rightarrow x \mathbin{R} z\)
reflexive / irreflexive: \(\forall x \in A\;(x \mathbin{R} x)\) / \(\forall x \in A\;(x \mathbin{\not\mathrel{R}} x)\)
trichotomy: \(\forall x, y \in A\;\bigl(x \mathbin{R} y \vee y \mathbin{R} x \vee x = y\bigr)\)
symmetric: \(x \mathbin{R} y \leftrightarrow y \mathbin{R} x\)

and the three composite notions we care about:


\(R\) (strictly) partially orders \(A\)

\(R\) is transitive and irreflexive on \(A\).

\(R\) (strictly) totally orders \(A\)

\(R\) is transitive, irreflexive, and satisfies trichotomy on \(A\).

\(R\) is an equivalence relation on \(A\)

\(R\) is transitive, reflexive, and symmetric on \(A\).



We take the strict \(<\) as basic and read \(x \le y\) as \(x < y \vee x = y\). For example, \(<\) on \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a strict total order; \(\le\) is not (it is not irreflexive).


Domain, range, restriction

\(\operatorname{dom}(R) := \{\,x : \exists y\,(\langle x, y\rangle \in R)\,\}\)
\(\operatorname{ran}(R) := \{\,y : \exists x\,(\langle x, y\rangle \in R)\,\}\)
\(R \restriction A := \{\,\langle x, y\rangle \in R : x \in A\,\}\)

The definitions are stated for an arbitrary set \(R\), not only for relations. The restriction \(R \restriction A\) is used mostly for functions.
Justification (these classes are sets). Recall \(\langle x, y\rangle =
\bigl\{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\bigr\}\). So if \(\langle x, y\rangle \in R\), then \(\{x\}\) and \(\{x, y\}\) lie in \(\bigcup R\), and hence \(x, y \in \bigcup\bigcup R\). Comprehension then gives
\[
\operatorname{dom}(R) = \bigl\{\,x \in \textstyle\bigcup\bigcup R : \exists y\,(\langle x, y\rangle \in R)\,\bigr\},
\]
and similarly for \(\operatorname{ran}(R)\).

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Functions
Definition (function). \(R\) is a function iff \(R\) is a relation and for every \(x \in \operatorname{dom}(R)\) there is a unique \(y\) with \(\langle x,
y\rangle \in R\); that unique \(y\) is written \(R(x)\).

\(F : A \to B\):   \(F\) is a function with \(\operatorname{dom}(F) = A\) and \(\operatorname{ran}(F) \subseteq B\).
\(F : A \xrightarrow[\text{onto}]{} B\):   \(F : A \to B\) and \(\operatorname{ran}(F) = B\) (a surjection).
\(F : A \xrightarrow{1\text{-}1} B\):   \(F : A \to B\) and \(\forall x, x' \in A\;\bigl(F(x) = F(x') \rightarrow x = x'\bigr)\) (an injection).
\(F : A \xrightarrow[\text{onto}]{1\text{-}1} B\):   both of the above (a bijection from \(A\) onto \(B\)).

Image of a set.
\[
F(A) \;=\; F{}''A \;=\; \operatorname{ran}(F \restriction A).
\]
The notation \(F(A)\) is standard but ambiguous when \(A\) happens to be both a member and a subset of \(\operatorname{dom}(F)\) — e.g. with \(\operatorname{dom}(F)
= 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}\), is \(F(2)\) the value at \(2\) or the image of \(\{0, 1\}\)? Write \(F{}''A\) when this could be confused.

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Building relations and functions
The axioms used so far (Extensionality, Comprehension, Pairing, Union) do not let us build many relations. The obvious source is the Cartesian product
\[
A \times B \;=\; \{\,\langle x, y\rangle : x \in A \wedge y \in B\,\},
\]
after which any relation between \(A\) and \(B\) is a subset of \(A \times B\), cut out by Comprehension. So everything reduces to: does \(A \times B\) exist?

First method: Power Set
If \(x \in A\) and \(y \in B\) then \(\{x\}, \{x, y\} \subseteq A \cup B\), so \(\langle x, y\rangle = \bigl\{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\bigr\} \in \mathcal{P}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)\bigr)\). Hence
\[
A \times B \;=\; \bigl\{\, w \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists x \in A\;\exists y \in B\;(w = \langle x, y\rangle)\,\bigr\}
\]
exists by Power Set (twice) and Comprehension.
This works, but it is a little “wasteful” in terms of cardinality. The sets
\[
\{0\} \times \omega, \qquad
\operatorname{id}_\omega = \{\,\langle x, x\rangle : x \in \omega\,\}
\]
have the same “size” as \(\omega\), yet the justification above manufactures them as subsets of \(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\omega))\) — a set of size \(2^{2^{\aleph_0}}\). We are invoking the existence of a huge set to produce a countable one.


Second method: Replacement

General method. Suppose \(\forall x \in A\;\exists! y\;\varphi(x, y)\). Then Replacement gives a set \(B\) with \(\forall x \in A\;\exists y \in B\;\varphi(x,
y)\), and Comprehension trims it to \(\{\,y \in B : \exists x \in A\;\varphi(x,
y)\,\} = \{\,y : \exists x \in A\;\varphi(x, y)\,\}\). So the image of a set under a definable single-valued relation is a set.

Apply this to build \(A \times B\) without Power Set. Fix \(b \in B\) and let
\[
\varphi(x, y) \;\equiv\; y = \langle x, b\rangle .
\]
Then \(\forall x \in A\;\exists! y\;\varphi(x, y)\), so by Replacement + Comprehension the set
\[
A \times \{b\} \;=\; \{\,\langle x, b\rangle : x \in A\,\}
\]
exists. Applying Replacement again — now over \(b \in B\) — gives
\[
S \;:=\; \bigl\{\, A \times \{b\} : b \in B\,\bigr\},
\]
and finally \(A \times B = \bigcup S\) by Union.

This argument never opened up \(\langle x, b\rangle\); it used only that \(\langle x, b\rangle\) is some set determined by \(x\) and \(b\). So it proves \(A \times B\) (and also \(\operatorname{dom}(R)\), \(\operatorname{ran}(R)\)) exist for any definition of the ordered pair.

Packaging the general method as a statement about functions:

Lemma. If \(\forall x \in A\;\exists! y\;\varphi(x, y)\), then there is a function \(f\) with \(\operatorname{dom}(f) = A\) such that for each \(x \in A\), \(f(x)\) is the unique \(y\) with \(\varphi(x, y)\).

Proof. Fix \(B\) from Replacement and set \(f = \{\,\langle x, y\rangle \in A
\times B : \varphi(x, y)\,\}\). \(\square\)

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Inverses, composition, isomorphism


\(R^{-1} := \{\,\langle y, x\rangle : \langle x, y\rangle \in R\,\}\)

a subset of \(\operatorname{ran}(R) \times \operatorname{dom}(R)\). If \(f\) is a function, \(f^{-1}\) is a function iff \(f\) is \(1\)-\(1\).

\(G \circ F := \{\,\langle x, z\rangle : \exists y\,(\langle x, y\rangle \in F \wedge \langle y, z\rangle \in G)\,\}\)

when \(F, G\) are functions with \(\operatorname{ran}(F) \subseteq
\operatorname{dom}(G)\), this is just \((G \circ F)(x) = G(F(x))\).



Isomorphism. Let \(R\) be a binary relation on \(A\) and \(S\) a binary relation on \(B\). Then \(F\) is an isomorphism from \((A, R)\) onto \((B, S)\) iff
\[
F : A \xrightarrow[\text{onto}]{1\text{-}1} B
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall x, y \in A\;\bigl[\,x \mathbin{R} y \leftrightarrow F(x) \mathbin{S} F(y)\,\bigr].
\]
We write \((A, R) \cong (B, S)\) when such an \(F\) exists. The definition makes sense for arbitrary relations; for now we use it for orderings.

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Equivalence relations and quotients
Let \(R\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(A\), and \(x \in A\). Define
\[
[x] \;:=\; \{\,y \in A : x \mathbin{R} y\,\}
\qquad\text{(Comprehension)},
\]
the equivalence class of \(x\), and
\[
A / R \;:=\; \bigl\{\, [x] : x \in A\,\bigr\}.
\]
To see \(A/R\) is a set, apply the general method with \(\varphi(x, y) \equiv y =
[x]\): by Lemma I.7.9 there is a function \(f\) with \(\operatorname{dom}(f) = A\) and \(f(x) = [x]\) — the quotient map \(x \mapsto [x]\) — and then \(A/R =
\operatorname{ran}(f)\).
This is the standard justification, in books on group theory and topology, for forming a quotient of a structure by an equivalence relation; the extra structure on \(A/R\) is defined separately.

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Object theory versus metatheory
The informal notions “relation” and “function” get two representations in set theory: as sets (objects of the formal theory ZFC), and as abbreviations in the metatheory.

As sets
A relation is a specific kind of set, handled inside ZFC. The defining property is a formula of the object theory — for example
\[
\operatorname{Rel}(R) \;:\equiv\; \forall u \in R\;\exists y, z\;\bigl(u = \langle y, z\rangle\bigr).
\]
We then prove facts about such sets as theorems of ZFC, e.g.
\[
\mathrm{ZFC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Rel}(R) \rightarrow \exists z\,\bigl(z = \operatorname{dom}(R)\bigr),
\]
using the justification given earlier. A concrete function such as \(f = \{\langle
1, 2\rangle, \langle 2, 2\rangle, \langle 3, 1\rangle\}\) is likewise a set formally defined in ZFC.


As abbreviations in the metatheory
By contrast, \(\in\), \(=\), \(\subseteq\) are informal relations — a different kind of animal. The “relation”
\[
S \;=\; \{\,p : \exists x, y\;(p = \langle x, y\rangle \wedge x \subseteq y)\,\}
\]
does not exist: it is a proper class, since \(\operatorname{dom}(S)\) would be the universe \(V\). We view \(x \subseteq y\) instead as an abbreviation in the metatheory for \(\forall z\,(z \in x \rightarrow z \in y)\); likewise \((A, R)
\cong (B, S)\) abbreviates a longer statement. Membership and equality, \(\in\) and \(=\), are already primitive symbols.
Many properties from the terminology list still make sense for such pseudorelations, by plugging them into the defining formula. For instance \(\in\) totally orders \(3 = \{0, 1, 2\}\) (i.e. \(\forall x, y, z \in 3\,[x \in y
\wedge y \in z \rightarrow x \in z]\), plus trichotomy), while \(\subseteq\) is transitive on all of \(V\) but not a total order of \(3\), and \(\in\) is not transitive on \(V\) (since \(0 \in \{0\} \in \{\{0\}\}\) but \(0 \notin \{\{0\}\}\)).
Similarly for functions: \(\bigcup : V \to V\) and \(\mathcal{P} : V \to V\) are pseudofunctions. There is no set of pairs \(\bigcup = \{\langle \mathcal{F},
\bigcup \mathcal{F}\rangle : \mathcal{F} \in V\}\); instead there is a formula \(\varphi(\mathcal{F}, Z)\) saying “\(Z\) is the union of the members of \(\mathcal{F}\)”, we prove \(\forall \mathcal{F}\;\exists! Z\;\varphi(\mathcal{F},
Z)\), and \(\bigcup \mathcal{F}\) denotes that \(Z\). Function properties still apply as abbreviations — e.g. “\(\bigcup\) is not \(1\)-\(1\)” is the formula
\[
\exists x_1, x_2, y\;\bigl[\varphi(x_1, y) \wedge \varphi(x_2, y) \wedge x_1 \neq x_2\bigr].
\]

title: Cofinality and Inaccessible Cardinals
text:
Recall two basic facts about cardinalities:

Finite unions of finite sets are finite.
Countable unions of countable sets are countable (using \(\mathsf{AC}\)).

This means it is “hard” to reach the cardinals \(\aleph_0\) and \(\aleph_1\) “from below”: you cannot obtain a set of size \(\aleph_0\) by putting together a few small pieces, and similarly for \(\aleph_1\). The notion of cofinality quantifies “how hard” it is to reach an ordinal from below.
Throughout this section, \({}\alpha\) denotes a limit ordinal (following Kunen, Def. I.13.10, we define cofinality only for limit ordinals).







Definition 1 
A set \(X \subseteq \alpha\) is cofinal in \({}\alpha\) if \[
    \forall \gamma < \alpha \; \exists \xi \in X \;\; \gamma < \xi.
\] Equivalently, \[
    \alpha = \bigcup_{\xi \in X} \xi = \sup X.
\]











Definition 2 
The cofinality of \({}\alpha\) is \[
    \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) = \text{least ordinal } \beta \text{ such that there exists } f: \beta \to \alpha \text{ with } \operatorname{ran}(f) \text{ cofinal in } \alpha.
\] We call such an \(f\) a cofinal map.




We can always assume that a cofinal map \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) is strictly increasing: if necessary, we can “thin it out”.







Lemma 1 
There exists a strictly increasing cofinal map \(g: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be cofinal. Define \(g\) by recursion: \[
    g(\eta) = \max\left\{ f(\eta), \; \sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} \right\}.
\] We have to check that \(g(\eta) < \alpha\). If \(\sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} = \alpha\), then \(g\mid_{\eta}\) would be a cofinal map from \(\eta < \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) into \({}\alpha\) (here we use that \({}\alpha\) is a limit), contradicting the minimality of \(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\). By construction, \(g\) is strictly increasing, and \(g(\eta) \geq f(\eta)\) implies that \(g\) is cofinal.











Example 1 


\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega) = \omega\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega+\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega + n\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega\cdot\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega \cdot n\)












Proposition 1 
For any limit ordinal \({}\alpha\),

\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \leq \alpha\),
\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) is a cardinal,
\(\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)) = \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).











NoteProof






Proof.

(\(\mathsf{AC}\)) Let \((\kappa_i)_{i\in I}\) and \((\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\) be families of cardinals such that \(\kappa_i < \lambda_i\) for all \(i \in I\). Then \[

\end{align*}\] where the last equality uses \(\delta \leq \kappa\). This is a contradiction.

\end{align*}\]

\end{equation*}\]

\[

\]

Suppose \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible and \(x\subseteq V_\kappa\). Then
\[

\]

Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(x \in V_\kappa\), then \(x \in V_\alpha\) for some \(\alpha < \kappa\), and by transitivity \(x \subseteq V_\alpha\). By the proof of Proposition 5, \(|x| \leq |V_\alpha| < \kappa\).

\[

We have already seen that for limit \(\alpha > \omega\), \(V_\alpha\) is a model of all \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) axioms except Replacement.

If \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\).










NoteProof

Suppose an inaccessible cardinal exists, and let \({}\kappa\) be the least inaccessible.
It is not hard to verify that
\[

\]
(You verify that being an inaccessible cardinal is absolute for \(V_\kappa\).) Therefore, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is not provable from \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This fact also follows from Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem.

Finite unions of finite sets are finite.

A set \(X \subseteq \alpha\) is cofinal in \({}\alpha\) if \[
    \forall \gamma < \alpha \; \exists \xi \in X \;\; \gamma < \xi.
\] Equivalently, \[
    \alpha = \bigcup_{\xi \in X} \xi = \sup X.
\]

The cofinality of \({}\alpha\) is \[
    \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) = \text{least ordinal } \beta \text{ such that there exists } f: \beta \to \alpha \text{ with } \operatorname{ran}(f) \text{ cofinal in } \alpha.
\] We call such an \(f\) a cofinal map.




We can always assume that a cofinal map \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) is strictly increasing: if necessary, we can “thin it out”.

There exists a strictly increasing cofinal map \(g: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be cofinal. Define \(g\) by recursion: \[
    g(\eta) = \max\left\{ f(\eta), \; \sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} \right\}.
\] We have to check that \(g(\eta) < \alpha\). If \(\sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} = \alpha\), then \(g\mid_{\eta}\) would be a cofinal map from \(\eta < \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) into \({}\alpha\) (here we use that \({}\alpha\) is a limit), contradicting the minimality of \(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\). By construction, \(g\) is strictly increasing, and \(g(\eta) \geq f(\eta)\) implies that \(g\) is cofinal.











Example 1 


\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega) = \omega\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega+\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega + n\)

\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \leq \alpha\),

\(\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)) = \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).

Proof. 

The identity map \(\alpha \to \alpha\) is cofinal.

For the other inequality, let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be strictly increasing and cofinal (Lemma 1), and let \(g: \delta \to \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) be cofinal. Then \(f \circ g: \delta \to \alpha\) is cofinal: given \(\gamma < \alpha\), pick \(\eta\) with \(f(\eta) > \gamma\), and \(\zeta < \delta\) with \(g(\zeta) > \eta\). Then \(f(g(\zeta)) > f(\eta) > \gamma\). Hence \(\delta \geq \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).

If \(\lambda < \kappa\) is a limit, then \(V_\lambda\) is a union of \(|\lambda| < \kappa\) many sets, each of size \(< \kappa\), so by regularity of \({}\kappa\), \(|V_\lambda| < \kappa\).




This in turn implies we can bound the cardinality of elements of \(V_\kappa\).







Proposition 6 
Suppose \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible and \(x\subseteq V_\kappa\). Then
\[
    x \in V_\kappa \; \Leftrightarrow \; |x| < \kappa.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(x \in V_\kappa\), then \(x \in V_\alpha\) for some \(\alpha < \kappa\), and by transitivity \(x \subseteq V_\alpha\). By the proof of Proposition 5, \(|x| \leq |V_\alpha| < \kappa\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Since \(x \subseteq V_\kappa\), each \(y \in x\) has rank \(< \kappa\). Since \(|x| < \kappa\), by regularity of \({}\kappa\),
\[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \sup\{\operatorname{rank}(y)+1 \colon y \in x\} < \kappa
\]
which implies \(x \in V_\kappa\).




We have already seen that for limit \(\alpha > \omega\), \(V_\alpha\) is a model of all \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) axioms except Replacement.







Theorem 2 
If \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We verify that \(V_\kappa\) satisfies the axiom of Replacement. Suppose \(x \in V_\kappa\) and \(f:x \to V_\kappa\) is a function. Then \(f[x] \subseteq V_\kappa\), and by Proposition 6, \(|f[x]| \leq |x| < \kappa\). Applying the other direction of Proposition 6 to \(f[x]\), we obtain \(f[x] \in V_\kappa\), as desired.




Suppose an inaccessible cardinal exists, and let \({}\kappa\) be the least inaccessible.
It is not hard to verify that
\[
V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}+ \text{``there does not exist an inaccessible cardinal''}.
\]
(You verify that being an inaccessible cardinal is absolute for \(V_\kappa\).) Therefore, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is not provable from \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This fact also follows from Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
text: These notes accompany Lecture 3. They expand the handwritten notes and follow Kunen, The Foundations of Mathematics, §0.4 and §I.1–I.6. Where Lecture 2 ended — Hilbert’s program — is where we begin.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
section: From Hilbert’s program to a working foundation
text:
From Hilbert’s program to a working foundation
Hilbert’s response to the foundational crisis was formalism: not the claim that mathematics is a meaningless game with symbols, but a method. Take a mathematical theory, write its axioms in a formal language, and study its formal proof-structure with modest, uncontroversial means. This method forces a distinction that will organize everything that follows.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
text:
Metatheory and object theory
Formalism introduces a split between two levels of discourse.

The two levels








Object theory (formal theory)
Metatheory




Example
a theory of arithmetic, or ZFC itself
our reasoning about that theory


Status
a combinatorial object: sets of symbols, strings, rules
ordinary mathematical reasoning


Language
a fixed formal language, e.g. first-order logic
informal natural language


“Proof”
a finite symbolic derivation
an intuitively convincing argument




The object theory is formalized
To say the object theory is formalized means two things:

its axioms are expressed in a formal language (for us, first-order logic with ∈);
its theorems are deduced in a purely symbolic fashion — as Kleene put it, like a list of chess moves written in chess notation. Whether a string is a correct proof is decided by inspecting symbols, not by understanding meaning.

A consequence Hilbert exploited: once proofs are finite strings manipulated by explicit rules, the combinatorics of proof becomes essentially elementary arithmetic. Reasoning about proofs is reasoning about finite syntactic objects.


Reasoning in the metatheory
The metatheory is where we actually work when we prove things about the formal system. That reasoning is:

informal — carried out in natural language;
intuitively clear and convincing — it must persuade without itself being formalized;
finitistic — close to elementary number theory. We do not treat infinite totalities as completed wholes unless they can be clearly and explicitly specified. In flavour this is the intuitionist / constructivist standpoint: an existence claim should come with a construction.



A finitistic statement, and a non-statement
Consider the claim
\[
P \text{ and } \mathbb{N}\setminus P \text{ are both infinite,}
\qquad P = \{\text{primes}\}.
\]
This is a statement involving completed infinite sets (i.e. it is a statement about the natural numbers as a whole). But it can be rewritten finitistically:

For every natural number \(n > 1\) there is a composite number \(c\) with \(n < c \le 2n\), and a prime \(p\) with \(n < p \le n! + 1\).

Both witnesses are bounded (and even can be explicitely defined). This is the kind of fact the metatheory is entitled to assert.
Contrast this with
\[
|\mathbb{R}| = |\mathbb{C}|,
\]
which is meaningless in the metatheory — it is a statement about the cardinality of uncountable sets, with no finitistic content. It only makes sense inside an object theory such as ZFC.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
section: The foundational loop: formalizing the metatheory
text:
The foundational loop: formalizing the metatheory

For a foundational theory such as ZFC, the formal (object) theory should be strong enough to formalize its own metatheory. Otherwise the reasoning we use to study ZFC would sit outside the foundation ZFC claims to provide.

This motivates a thesis about ZFC — a property we would want a foundation to have:

Thesis. Every finitistic fact can be formalized and proved within ZFC.

Making this precise takes care, because most everyday mathematical statements are not literally in the language of ZFC. For instance
\[
\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\;\bigl(x^{3}\cdot x^{5} = x^{8}\bigr)
\]
uses \(\mathbb{R}\), multiplication, and exponentiation — none of which are primitive symbols of a language whose only non-logical symbol is ∈. Such statements enter ZFC through codings / representations.

Example: an arithmetic fact and its formal shadow
“\(2 + 8 = 10\)” is a fact of the metatheory. Inside ZFC we find:

a representation of each natural number as a specific set — write \(\ulcorner 2 \urcorner\), \(\ulcorner 8 \urcorner\), \(\ulcorner 10 \urcorner\);
a defined binary function symbol \(+\) for addition of such representations;

and then we can prove
\[
\mathrm{ZFC} \;\vdash\; \ulcorner 2 \urcorner + \ulcorner 8 \urcorner
= \ulcorner 10 \urcorner .
\]
The metatheoretic fact and its formal counterpart are different objects; the thesis says the second always tracks the first.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
text:
ZFC as a foundational theory
The claim that ZFC founds mathematics rests on two theses:

All abstract mathematical concepts are set-theoretical.
All concrete mathematical objects are specific sets.

If one does not accept formalism, the “are” can be weakened to “have set-theoretical representations.”

Everything reduces to sets.


Example: what a function is
\[
\text{function} \;\cong\; \text{graph} \;\cong\;
\text{a set of ordered pairs } f \text{ with }
\forall x, y, z\,\bigl((x,y)\in f \wedge (x,z)\in f \rightarrow y = z\bigr).
\]
This pushes the question back to ordered pairs, which are themselves described as special kinds of sets — the standard choice being
\[
(x, y) := \bigl\{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\bigr\},
\]
for which one verifies \((x,y) = (x',y') \rightarrow (x = x' \wedge y = y')\).


The special nature of the ZFC axioms
Kunen distinguishes axioms used as statements of faith (obviously true facts, as the Greeks viewed Euclid’s postulates) from definitional axioms (merely delimiting a useful class of structures, as with the group axioms).
You can read the ZFC axioms in the first sense: To a Platonist, these might appear as obviously true facts. But we have seen that an all too careless treatment of the notion of set can lead to contradictions. However, one can, independent of the ontological status of the axioms, read ZFC as the theory of everything: one postulates the ZFC axioms once and for all, and every other axiom system — groups, rings, topological spaces — is defined inside it.


What we will do

The basic level. State the axioms and interpret them; work out what exactly the representations of \(3\) and of \(\mathbb{R}\) are. (Following von Neumann, \(0 = \varnothing\), \(1 = \{\varnothing\}\), \(2 = \{0,1\}\), \(3 = \{0,1,2\}\), …, \(\mathbb{N} = \omega\); and \(\mathbb{R}\) via Dedekind cuts.)
The advanced level. Draw out the consequences of the axioms for uncountable sets.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
text:
The axioms of ZFC
The language is first-order logic with a single binary relation symbol ∈ (and equality). There is one sort of variable: everything ranges over sets. In the Union and Replacement axioms below, the capital letters \(A, Y,
\mathcal{F}, B\) are still just set variables — the capitals only aid reading.
Convention. Every axiom is understood to be universally quantified over its free variables (\(\forall x\,\forall y\,\dots\)).


Axiom 0 — Set Existence

\(\exists x\,(x = x)\)

Axiom 1 — Extensionality

\(\forall z\,(z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) \;\rightarrow\; x = y\)


A set is determined by its members.

Axiom 2 — Foundation

\(\exists y\,(y \in x) \;\rightarrow\;
\exists y\,\bigl(y \in x \wedge \neg\exists z\,(z \in x \wedge z \in y)\bigr)\)


Every nonempty set has an ∈-minimal element; no infinite descending ∈-chains.

Axiom 3 — Comprehension (Separation) — scheme

For each formula \(\varphi\) with \(y\) not free: \(\exists y\,\forall x\,\bigl(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \in v \wedge
\varphi(x)\bigr)\)


Subsets are carved out of a set \(v\) that already exists — the restriction to \(x \in v\) is what defuses Russell’s paradox (there is no universal set). There is one axiom per formula, so this is infinitely many axioms; that is harmless in the metatheory, since “being a formula” is a finitistically decidable property.

Axiom 4 — Pairing

\(\exists z\,(x \in z \wedge y \in z)\)

Axiom 5 — Union

\(\exists A\,\forall Y\,\forall x\,
\bigl(x \in Y \wedge Y \in \mathcal{F} \;\rightarrow\; x \in A\bigr)\)

Axiom 6 — Replacement — scheme

For each formula \(\varphi\) with \(B\) not free: \(\forall x \in A\;\exists! y\,\varphi(x, y) \;\rightarrow\;
\exists B\,\forall x \in A\;\exists y \in B\;\varphi(x, y)\)


The image of a set under a definable class function is a set. Here \(\exists! y\,\varphi(x,y)\) abbreviates \(\exists y\,\bigl(\varphi(x,y) \wedge \forall z\,(\varphi(x,z) \rightarrow
y = z)\bigr)\). Again a scheme, and again finitistically unproblematic.




Some defined symbols
On the basis of Axioms 1, 3, 4, 5 we abbreviate:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \subseteq y \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall z\,(z \in x \rightarrow z \in y)\\[2pt]
x = \varnothing \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall z\,(z \notin x)\\[2pt]
y = S(x) \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow z \in x \vee z = x)
     \qquad\bigl(\,y = x \cup \{x\}\,\bigr)\\[2pt]
y = v \cap w \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall x\,(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \in v \wedge x \in w)\\[2pt]
\mathrm{SING}(x) \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \exists y \in x\;\forall z \in x\,(z = y)
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining axioms are easier to state with these in hand.


Axiom 7 — Infinity

\(\exists x\,\bigl(\varnothing \in x \wedge \forall y \in x\,(S(y) \in x)\bigr)\)


There is a set containing \(\varnothing\) and closed under \(y \mapsto y \cup
\{y\}\). Here “\(\varnothing \in x\)” abbreviates \(\exists y\,(y = \varnothing
\wedge y \in x)\), and “\(S(y) \in x\)” abbreviates \(\exists z\,(z = S(y) \wedge
z \in x)\).

Axiom 8 — Power Set

\(\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \subseteq x \rightarrow z \in y)\)

Axiom 9 — Choice (AC)

\(\varnothing \notin F \wedge \forall x \in F\;\forall y \in F\,
(x \neq y \rightarrow x \cap y = \varnothing) \;\rightarrow\;
\exists C\;\forall x \in F\;\mathrm{SING}(C \cap x)\)


For a family \(F\) of pairwise disjoint nonempty sets there is a set \(C\) meeting each member in exactly one point.





Named subsystems







System
Axioms




ZFC
1–9


ZF
1–8 (no Choice)


ZC
ZFC without Replacement (6)


Z
ZF without Replacement (6)



Other important subsystems:

\(X^{-}\) — drop Foundation (2);
\(X{-}\mathrm{P}\) — drop Power Set (8);
\(X{-}\mathrm{Inf}\) — drop Infinity (7).

Most of elementary mathematics can be carried out in \(\mathrm{ZC}^{-}\). A minimal working fragment is Basic Set Theory:
\[
\mathrm{BST} \;=\; \text{Axioms } 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \;+\; (6 \vee 8).
\]

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text: We take the axioms of ZFC as given and start deriving things — beginning with Axioms 1, 3, 4, 5 (Extensionality, Comprehension, Pairing, Union).
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text:
Extensionality and Comprehension
Axiom 1 (Extensionality). A set is completely determined by its elements:
\[
\forall z\,(z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) \;\rightarrow\; x = y .
\]
This does more than it seems. It also fixes what our universe contains. If we allowed an object with no members that is not the empty set — a duck \(D\) and a badger \(B\), say — then \(\forall z\,(z \in B \leftrightarrow z \in D)\) would hold vacuously, forcing \(B = D = \varnothing\). So every object in our universe is a set, and hereditarily so: its members, their members, and so on are all sets. The universe of hereditary sets is informally called \(V\).
Axiom 3 (Comprehension / Separation). For each formula \(\varphi\) (with \(y\) not free),
\[
\forall v\;\exists y\;\forall x\,\bigl(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \in v \wedge
\varphi(x)\bigr).
\]
Subsets are separated out of a set that already exists. This restriction is the whole point, as the next section shows.
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text:
How Comprehension avoids Russell’s paradox
Naive comprehension — “for every property \(Q\), the set \(\{x : Q(x)\}\) exists” — is inconsistent. With \(Q(x) \equiv x \notin x\) we get Russell’s set \(R\) and the contradiction \(R \in R \leftrightarrow R \notin R\).
Under Axiom 3 we may only form, relative to a set \(v\),
\[
R_v \;=\; \{\,x \in v : x \notin x\,\}.
\]
Run Russell’s argument on this. If \(R_v \in v\), then \(R_v \in R_v
\leftrightarrow R_v \notin R_v\) — still a contradiction. The escape is that we are no longer forced into it: we simply conclude
\[
R_v \notin v .
\]
Since \(v\) was arbitrary, every set omits some object, and there is no set of all sets:

Theorem (no universal set). \(\;\forall v\;\exists R\;(R \notin v).\)

Whether this is a desirable feature is a fair question — a foundation in which “the collection of all sets” is not itself an object can feel like a defect. It is better read as the price of consistency: the same restriction that blocks Russell blocks the universal set.
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
section: Formal definitions versus their metatheoretic meaning
text:
Formal definitions versus their metatheoretic meaning
A defined symbol is introduced by a purely symbolic clause. For intersection:
\[
\mathrm{int}(a, b, y) \;:\Longleftrightarrow\;
\forall x\,\bigl(x \in y \leftrightarrow (x \in a \wedge x \in b)\bigr).
\]
Informally we read \(y = a \cap b\), but that reading lives in the metatheory. Before we are entitled to write the term \(a \cap b\), we must check that it names exactly one set:

Lemma. \(\;\forall a, b\;\exists! y\;\mathrm{int}(a, b, y).\)

Existence is Comprehension applied to \(v = a\) with \(\varphi(x) \equiv x \in a
\wedge x \in b\). Uniqueness is Extensionality: if \(\mathrm{int}(a,b,y)\) and \(\mathrm{int}(a,b,z)\), then \(\forall x\,(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \in z)\), hence \(y = z\).
This is the standard pattern. We name an operation (or a constant) only after proving that the defining formula is satisfied by exactly one set — just as one proves \(\sqrt{2}\) is the unique \(y > 0\) with \(y^2 = 2\) before using the notation.
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text:
Classes and the class-builder notation
Let \(\varphi(x)\) be any formula. Informally \(\{x : \varphi(x)\}\) is a class — this is just notation.

If there is a set \(A\) with \(\forall x\,(x \in A \leftrightarrow
\varphi(x))\), then \(A\) is unique by Extensionality; we write \(A = \{x :
\varphi(x)\}\) and say the class exists (is a set).
Otherwise \(\{x : \varphi(x)\}\) is a proper class — a figure of speech, not an object.

Two examples:
\[
\varphi(x) \equiv x \notin x
\qquad\rightsquigarrow\qquad
\mathrm{ZFC} \vdash \neg\exists y\,\forall x\,(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \notin
x),
\]
so Russell’s class is proper;
\[
\varphi(x) \equiv x = x
\qquad\rightsquigarrow\qquad
\neg\exists A\,\forall x\,(x \in A),
\]
so the universal class \(V = \{x : x = x\}\) is proper. Saying “\(V\) does not exist” is just another way of writing \(\neg\exists A\,\forall x\,(x \in A)\); there is no more of a puzzle here than in “trolls do not exist.”
Finally, \(\{x \in z : \varphi(x)\}\) abbreviates \(\{x : x \in z \wedge
\varphi(x)\}\), and Comprehension says these always exist.
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text:
Building sets from nothing

The empty set


\(\varnothing\)

the unique \(y\) with \(\forall z\,(z \notin y)\).



Existence: take any set (Axiom 0) and apply Comprehension with an always-false \(\varphi\), e.g. \(x \neq x\). Uniqueness: Extensionality. At this point \(\varnothing\) is the only specific set we have proved to exist.


Pairs
Pairing gives \(\exists z\,(x \in z \wedge y \in z)\); the \(z\) may have other elements, so trim it with Comprehension to \(\{w \in z : w = x \vee w = y\}\). This licenses:

\(\{x, y\} := \{w : w = x \vee w = y\}\)
\(\{x\} := \{x, x\}\)
\(\langle x, y \rangle = (x, y) := \bigl\{\{x\},\, \{x, y\}\bigr\}\)

The one property the ordered pair must have is
\[
\langle x, y \rangle = \langle x', y' \rangle \;\rightarrow\;
x = x' \wedge y = y'
\]
(prove it by splitting into the cases \(x = y\) and \(x \neq y\)). Any other definition with this property would serve equally well; the bracket notation \(\langle\,\cdot\,,\cdot\,\rangle\) marks that we mean this one.
We can now start counting:
\[
0 = \varnothing, \qquad
1 = \{0\} = \{\varnothing\}, \qquad
2 = \{0, 1\} = \bigl\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\bigr\}.
\]
The axioms so far generate infinitely many different sets — for example, \(\varnothing\), \(\{\varnothing\}\), \(\{\{\varnothing\}\}\), … — but none with more than two elements.


Union: getting bigger sets


Axiom 5 — Union

\(\forall \mathcal{F}\;\exists A\;\forall Y\;\forall x\,
\bigl(x \in Y \wedge Y \in \mathcal{F} \;\rightarrow\; x \in A\bigr)\)


\(\bigcup \mathcal{F} := \{x : \exists Y \in \mathcal{F}\;(x \in Y)\}\) — the members of members of \(\mathcal{F}\).
It exists: take \(A\) from the axiom and separate \(\{x \in A : \exists Y \in \mathcal{F}\,(x \in Y)\}\).
\(u \cup v :=  \bigcup \{u, v\}\)

The axiom is stated for arbitrary families so that it covers infinite unions too, not just \(u \cup v\).
Worked example: the number 3. We have \(0, 1, 2\). Then:

\(\{0, 1\}\) by Pairing;
\(\{2\} = \{2, 2\}\) by Pairing;
\(\mathcal{F} = \bigl\{\{0,1\},\, \{2\}\bigr\}\) by Pairing;
\(\bigcup \mathcal{F} = \{0, 1, 2\} =: 3\).

Equivalently \(3 = 2 \cup \{2\}\). In general the successor is
\[
S(x) = x \cup \{x\}, \qquad
3 = S(2),\quad 4 = S(3),\quad \dots
\]

title: Cardinals
text:
Cardinal numbers capture the notion of the cardinality of a set. We measure the cardinality of a set relative to other sets by saying sets \(a,b\) have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection between them.
We use the following notation: \[\begin{align*}
a \sim b \quad & : \Leftrightarrow \quad \text{ there exists a bijection } a \leftrightarrow b \\
a \preceq b \quad & : \Leftrightarrow \quad \text{ there exists an injection } a \hookrightarrow b \\
a \prec b \quad & : \Leftrightarrow \quad a \preceq b \; \wedge \; a \nsim b
\end{align*}\]
It is straightforward to show \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation and that \(\preceq\) is transitive. \(\preceq\) is obviously also reflexive. Relations that are reflexive and transitive are called preorders. If we mod out by \(\sim\), do we get a partial order? In other words, do we have antisymmetry in the form \[
a \preceq b \; \wedge \; b \preceq a \quad \overset{?}{\Rightarrow} \quad a \sim b.
\] This follows pretty easily if we use the Axiom of Choice (in form of the well-ordering principle \(\mathsf{WO}\)), but it is one of the few fundamental results in the theory of cardinality one can prove without using Choice.







Theorem 1 (Cantor-Schröder-Bernstein Theorem) 
Let \(a\) and \(b\) be sets. If there is an injection from \(a\) to \(b\) and an injection from \(b\) to \(a\), then there exists a bijection between \(a\) and \(b\).











Exercise 1 (Warmup) Find a bijection between \([0,1)\) and \([0,1]\).











NoteProof






Proof. Let \(X_0 = X\setminus g(Y)\), \(Y_0 = Y \setminus f(X)\). Let \(X_1 = g(Y)\setminus g(f(X))\), \(Y_1 = f(X) \setminus f(g(Y))\). Note that there is a bijection between \(X_0 \cup X_1\) and \(Y_0 \cup Y_1\) by letting \[
\varphi(x) = \begin{cases}
  f(x) & \text{ if } x \in X_0, \\
  g^{-1}(x) & \text{ if } x \in X_1.
\end{cases}
\] Iterate this process with new \(X : = g(f(X))\) and \(Y := f(g(Y))\). This gives rise to sequences of pairwise disjoint sets \(X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots\) and \(Y_0, Y_1, Y_2, \dots\), together with a bijection \[
\varphi: \bigcup_{i \in \omega}  X_i \leftrightarrow \bigcup_{i \in \omega} Y_i.
\] We now define \[
h(x) = \begin{cases}
  \varphi(x) & \text{ if } x \in \bigcup_{i \in \omega}  X_i, \\
  f(x) & \text{ if } x \in X\setminus \bigcup_{i \in \omega}  X_i.
\end{cases}
\] It is clear that \(h\) is one-to-one. Suppose \(y \in Y \setminus \bigcup_{i \in \omega} Y_i\) is not in \(f(X\setminus \bigcup_{i \in \omega}  X_i)\). But then, by definition of \(\varphi\), \(y\) is not in \(f(Y)\), which would imply \(y \in Y_0\), contradiction. Hence \(h\) is onto.




The next result shows that this order is linear. To prove it, we have to use Choice.







Theorem 2 (Hartogs) 
For any sets \(a,b\), \[
a \preceq b \; \vee \; b \preceq a.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. By the well-ordering principle \(\mathsf{WO}\), there exist ordinals \(\alpha, \beta\) such that \(a \sim \alpha\) and \(b \sim \beta\). Since any two ordinals are comparable by \(<\), \(\alpha \subseteq \beta\) or \(\beta \subseteq \alpha\), which easily yields the theorem.




Cantor’s famous result shows that for every set there exists one with greater cardinality. In particular, the order \(\preceq\) is infinite. Given a set \(a\), we denote its power set by \(\mathcal{P}(a)\), \[
\mathcal{P}(a) = \{ b \colon b \subseteq a \}.
\]







Theorem 3 (Cantor’s Theorem) 
For every set \(a\), \[
a \prec \mathcal{P}(a).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. \(x \mapsto \{x\}\) is an injection from \(a\) to \(\mathcal{P}(a)\), hence \(a \preceq \mathcal{P}(a)\). Now assume \(a \sim \mathcal{P}(a)\) via a bijection \(f\). We use a diagonal argument (as for the case \(a = \mathbb{N}\)) to derive a contradiction. Let \(d: = \{x \in a\colon x \notin f(x) \}\). As \(f\) is onto, there exists \(b \in a\) with \(f(b) = d\). But then \[
b \in d \; \Leftrightarrow \; b \notin f(b) \; \Leftrightarrow \; b \notin d,
\] contradiction.







As with ordinals, we would like to choose a system of representatives for the equivalence classes under \(\sim\). Theorem 2 suggests to use ordinals (which we can compare using the well-ordering of ordinals). We therefore assume the Axiom of Choice (so every set has a well-ordering). One issue that remains is that a set can have well-orderings of different lengths (as we saw in the case of the natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\)). But since the ordinals are well-ordered, we can choose the least one of the same cardinality.







Definition 1 
The cardinality \(|a|\) of a set \(a\) is defined as \[
|a| = \min \{ \alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\colon \alpha \sim a \}.
\]











Remark 1. We have to be careful what we are taking a minimum over, since there could be a lot (i.e. “more than a set” many ordinals equinumeral to \(a\).) We can avoid this by first using \(\mathsf{AC}\) to find one ordinal \(\beta \sim a\), and then taking the minimum ordinals \(\leq \beta\). As we will see later, the latter will always be a set.











Lemma 1  

\(a \sim b \quad \iff \quad |a| = |b|\)
\(a \preceq b \quad \iff \quad |a| \leq |b|\)
\(a \prec b \quad \iff \quad |a| < |b|\)





An ordinal \({}\kappa\) is a cardinal if it is the cardinality of some set. Equivalently, \({}\kappa\) is a cardinal if \[
\forall \beta < \kappa \; \beta \prec \kappa.
\] We usually use Greek letters from the middle of the alphabet, \(\kappa, \mu, \nu, \dots\) to denote cardinals.
Given a cardinal \({}\kappa\), we let \(\kappa^+\) be the cardinal successor of \({}\kappa\), i.e.  \[
\kappa^+ = \text{ least cardinal } \nu \text{ with }  \kappa \prec \nu.
\] By Theorem 3 (and the Axiom of Choice), we have

We can draw some conclusions:

With \(|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{ \aleph_0}\) we also get \(|\mathbb{R}^n |\) = \((2^{ \aleph_0})^n = 2^{\aleph_0},\) by Hessenberg’s Theorem. It even holds that (exercise!) \[\begin{equation*}
|\{s \colon \mathbb{N}\to  \mathbb{R}\}|  =  (2^{ \aleph_0})^{\aleph_0} = 2^{ \aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0} = 2^{ \aleph_0}.
\end{equation*}\] That is, there are as many countable sequences of real numbers as there are real numbers.
Since every continuous real-valued function on \(\mathbb{R}\) is determined by its values on \(\mathbb{Q}\), we have \[
|\{f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\text{ continuous } \}| = |\{f:\mathbb{Q}\to \mathbb{R}\}| = (2^{ \aleph_0})^{\aleph_0} =  2^{ \aleph_0}.
\]
We obtain a higher cardinality by passing to the power set of the real numbers or to the set of all real-valued functions on \(\mathbb{R}\): \[\begin{equation*}
|\{f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\}| = |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})| =  2^{2^{ \aleph_0}} > 2^{ \aleph_0}.
\end{equation*}\]







ImportantContinuum Hypothesis (\(\mathsf{CH}\) – cardinal version)



\[
2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1
\]


\(\mathsf{CH}\) asserts that the cardinality of \(\mathbb{R}\) is the next biggest cardinal after \(\omega = \aleph_0\) (the cardinality of all countably infinite sets).

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text: A comparative study of the three dominant modern approaches to mathematical foundations: set theory (ZFC), category theory, and type theory (Martin-Löf dependent type theory, Homotopy Type Theory, Univalent Foundations). The course examines each framework on its own terms and then asks what it means to “found” mathematics at all.

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Lecture slides

1 · Some History and Setting the Stage — Bolzano, Dedekind, Cantor, Kronecker, Frege, Russell’s paradox.
2 · The Foundational Crisis — paradoxes and consistency, predicativity, the axiom of choice, intuitionism vs. Hilbert’s program.

title: Foundations of Mathematics

Notes

title: Models of Set Theory
text:
You may have noticed that, when introducing the axioms of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), we never really answered the question “What is a set?” Instead, we developed a formal theory of axioms for a binary relation that somehow describe “how sets work”, that is, how we can obtain sets from given ones using well-known operations like power set and union.
We have then seen how we can develop a lot of standard mathematical objects (like \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{R}\)) and techniques (like induction and definition by recursion) inside this formal system. In fact, most of mathematics can be developed formally inside this system. Almost all proofs you find in any standard math book are proofs that can be formalized in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). It is very tedious to do this for us humans, but there is little doubt it can be done, and in fact, looking at the recent work on proof assistants (like Coq or Lean), many parts of mathematics have been formalized (albeit not directly in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\)).
This expressiveness gives \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) its foundational importance, but it is also the cause for much confusion for someone who first studies set theory.
From a pedagogical point of view, in what follows it is helpful to assume a “Platonist” perspective of mathematics, and set theory in particular, namely that sets and the relations between exist independently (and outside) of the \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) axioms. The set of real numbers exists, and our development of \(\mathbb{R}\) inside \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is just a formal way to describe them. From this perspective, the axioms of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) (\(\mathsf{AC}\) is a little different) are just obvious truths about sets, just like the Peano axioms are obvious truths about natural numbers.
Among other things, this perspective allows us to treat \(\mathsf{ZF}\) just like any other mathematical theory, like group theory or the theory of algebraically closed fields. In particular, we can think about models of set theory the way we would think about models of group theory, in the sense of model theory.
A model would simply be a set \(M\) together with a binary relation \(E\) on \(S\) such that
\[
    (M,E) \models \mathsf{ZF},
\]
that is, all axioms hold when interpreted in \((M,E)\). Note that we use “set” in this context not in the formal sense, but in the “meta”-sense (the Platonist world of sets).
Working in the meta-theory (“that what is mathematically true”), we know by Gödel’s completeness theorem that
  if \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent, then it has a model.
This model should be seen as a set-theoretic universe: Its elements can be seen as sets, and the interpretation \(E\) of the \(\in\)-symbol will tell us how these sets are connected via the element-relation.
Note that \(E\) does not have to be the actual element relation on a set (of sets), but just some binary relation so that the axioms are satisfied.
In the meta-world, there are, of course, sets other than \(M\), but that does not matter here, since all we are interested in is giving some universe in which our axioms hold. (Timothy Chow has suggested that set theory should rather be called “universe theory. He is right in the sense that what axiomatic set theory does is to define such universes of sets, rather than what a set is.)
In the meta-theory, we can then follow the usual techniques to show provability or non-provability results.
If we want to prove that \(\mathsf{CH}\) is consistent with \(\mathsf{ZF}\) (assuming \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent), we need to find a model in which both hold.
One difficulty in working with models of set theory is that they can look very different depending on whether you look at a model “from the inside” or “from the outside”.
To illustrate this, assume \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent. Then, by the Löwenheim-Skolem theorem, there exists a countable model for \(\mathsf{ZF}\). Yet it is a theorem of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) that there exists an uncountable set. This is often referred to as Skolem’s paradox, although it is not really an antinomy.
If we break this down a bit, we see that the apparent paradox is really just a matter of perspective (inside or outside). Assume \((M,E)\) is a countable model of \(\mathsf{ZF}\). Then there exists \(x \in M\) such that there is no injection from \(x\) to the natural numbers. Since \(M\) is countable, \(x\) can have at most countably many elements. So why is this not a contradiction? We should really read the statement above as
  there is no injection in \(M\) from \(x\) to \(M\)’s version of the natural numbers.
In other words, even though \(x\) is countable from the outside, \(x\) appears uncountable inside \(M\) since a mapping witnessing its countability does not exist in \(M\).
This is a first warning sign that models of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) can behave in very unexpected ways. For another example, recall the axiom of Foundation asserts that the \(\in\)-relation is well-founded. But again, this means only “from the inside”.







Proposition 1 
If \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent, then there exists a model \((M,E)\) of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) such that \((M,E)\) is ill-founded.










NoteProof






Proof. Introduce new constant symbols \(c_n\) \((n \in \mathbb{N})\) and add the formulas \(\varphi_n \equiv c_{n+1} \in c_n\) to the axioms of \(\mathsf{ZF}\). It is not hard to show, using the compactness theorem, that \(\mathsf{ZF}+ \bigcup_n \varphi_n\) has a model \((M^*, E^*)\), for which the set \(\{c_n \colon n \in \mathbb{N}\}\) is ill-founded.




Since, as mentioned above, the model \((M^*,E^*)\) satisfies Foundation, the set \(\{c_n \colon n \in \mathbb{N}\}\) is actually not in the model (and neither can be any other set with an infinite descending \(\in\)-chain).


If we restrict ourselves to models on which the \(E\)-relation is actually well-founded (i.e. from the outside), then interestingly these models look, in a way, “natural”: They can be assumed to be the \(\in\)-relation on a set. Such models are also called standard.
Given a set theoretic structure \((M,E)\) (not necessarily a model of \(\mathsf{ZF}\)), for each \(x \in M\) let \[\begin{equation*}
    \operatorname{ext}_E(x) = \{ y \in X \colon y\, E \, x \}
\end{equation*}\]
If \(E\) behaves “set-like”, then it will respect the axiom of Extensionality, i.e. two sets are identical if and only if they have the same elements. Therefore we say that \(E\) is extensional if \[\begin{equation*}
    x,z \in X, \; x\neq z \quad \text{ implies } \quad \operatorname{ext}_E(x) \neq \operatorname{ext}_E(z).
\end{equation*}\]
Furthermore, as stated above, we want to exclude infinite descending \(E\)-chains. Recall we say that \(E\) is well-founded if

every non-empty set \(Y \subseteq X\) has an \(E\)-minimal element.








Theorem 1 (Mostowski collapse) 
If \(E\) is an extensional and well-founded relation on a set \(X\), then there exists a transitive set \(S\) and a bijection \(\pi: X \to S\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    x \, E \, y \iff \pi(x) \in \pi(y) \quad \text{ for all $ x,y \in X$}.      
\end{equation*}\] Moreover, \(S\) and \({}\pi\) are unique.










NoteProof






Proof. We construct \({}\pi\) and \(S = \operatorname{im}(\pi)\) by recursion on \(E\), which is possible since it is well-founded.
For each \(x \in X\), let \[\begin{equation*}
    \pi(x) = \{\pi(y) \colon y \, E \, x \},
\end{equation*}\] and set \(S = \operatorname{ran}(\pi)\).
The injectivity of \({}\pi\) follows from the extensionality of \({}\pi\) by induction along \(E\):
Suppose we have shown \[\begin{equation*}
\forall z \; (z E x \to \forall y  \in X (\pi(z) = \pi(y) \to z = y)).
\end{equation*}\] and we have to show that it holds for \(x\). Assume \(\pi(x) = \pi(y)\) for some \(y \in X\). Then \[\begin{align*}
cEx &\Rightarrow& \pi(c) \in \pi(x) = \pi(y) &\\
&\Rightarrow& \pi(c) = \pi(z) & \qquad \text{ for some } zEy\\
&\Rightarrow& c=z & \qquad  (\text{by ind. hyp., since } cEx)\\
&\Rightarrow& cEy &.
\end{align*}\] Similarly, we get \(cEy \Rightarrow cEx\), hence \(x=y\) as desired due to the extensionality of \(E\). Finally we have \[\begin{align*}
\pi(x) \in \pi(y) & \Rightarrow & \pi(x) = \pi(c) & \qquad \text{ for some } cEy \\
&\Rightarrow& x = c & \qquad \text{ (since ${}\pi$ is injective)}\\
&\Rightarrow& xEy &
\end{align*}\] Thus \({}\pi\) is an isomorphism.
To see the uniqueness of \({}\pi\) and \(S\), assume \(\rho\), \(T\) are such that the statement of the theorem is satisfied. Then \(\pi \circ \rho^{-1}\) is an isomorphism between \((T, \in)\) and \((S,\in)\). Now apply the following lemma.











Lemma 1 
Suppose \(X,Y\) are sets, and \({}\theta\) is an isomorphism between \((X,\in)\) and \((Y,\in)\). Then \(X=Y\) and \(\theta(x) = x\) for all \(x \in X\).










NoteProof






Proof. By induction on the well-founded relation \(\in\). Assume that \(\theta(z)=z\) for all \(z \in x\) and let \(y = \theta(x)\).
We have \(x \subseteq y\) because if \(z \in x\), then \(z = \theta(z) \in \theta(x) = y\).
We also have \(y \subseteq x\): Let \(t \in y\). Since \(y \in Y\), there is \(z \in X\) with \(\theta(z) = t\). Since \(\theta(z) \in y\) and \(y = \theta(x)\), we have \(z \in x\), and thus \(t = \theta(z) = z \in x\).
Hence \(x = y\), and this also implies \(\theta(x) = x\).











Corollary 1 
If \(E\) is a well-order on a set \(X\), then \((X,E)\) is isomorphic to \((\alpha, \in)\) for a unique ordinal \(\alpha\).










NoteProof






Proof. Every linear order is extensional. Hence we can apply the Mostowski Collapse. It is easy to see that the resulting set is an ordinal.







Even if we consider well-founded standard models, interpreting set-theoretic statements in them can still lead to very different results, even for very simple formulas.







Example 1 
Consider \(M = \{0, \{\{0\}\}\}\) and let \(\varphi \equiv \{\{0\}\} \subseteq 0\). Clearly \({}\varphi\) is not true from the “outside”. But what if we look at it from “inside” \(M\)? \(x \subseteq y\) means \(\forall z (z \in x \to z \in y)\). Inside \(M\) this means every set \(z\) in \(M\) that is an element of \(x\) is also an element of \(y\). But in \(M\), there is no element \(z \in \{\{0\}\}\), \(\{0\}\) is not an element of \(M\). Therefore, \[
    (M, \in) \models \{\{0\}\} \subseteq 0.
\]




In the example above, the set \(M\) is not transitive, which allowed it to “hide” its elements. It turns out that if we require our model to be transitive, the truth of simple formulas cannot vary between the “inside” and the “outside” perspective. We call such properties absolute.
Given a formula \({}\varphi\) and some class \(M\), we can relativize \({}\varphi\) with respect to \(M\) essentially by restricting all quantifiers in \({}\varphi\) to range over \(M\), i.e. \(\exists x\) becomes \(\exists x \in M\) and \(\forall x\) becomes \(\forall x \in M\). Note that classes are defined by formulas, so the resulting formula, which we denote by \(\varphi^M\), is still a formula of set theory.







Definition 1 
We say a formula \(\varphi(x_0, \ldots, x_n)\) is absolute for a class \(M\) if for all \(a_0, \ldots, a_n \in M\) \[
    \varphi^M(a_0, \ldots, a_n) \text{ holds} \iff  \varphi(a_0, \ldots, a_n) \text{ holds}.
\]











Exercise 1 If \(M\) is transitive, then for all \({}\varphi\), \[
    (M, \in) \models \varphi \; \iff \; \varphi^M \text{ holds}.
\]











Definition 2 
A formula \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_0\) if it has no quantifiers or every quantifier of \({}\varphi\) is of the form \(\exists x \in y\) or \(\forall x \in y\) (i.e. every quantifier is bounded).











Lemma 2 
If \(M\) is transitive and \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_0\), then \({}\varphi\) is absolute for \(M\).










NoteProof






Proof. Clearly \(x=y\) and \(x\in y\) are absolute for any \(M\). It is also not hard to see that if \({}\varphi\) and \({}\psi\) are absolute for \(M\), then so are \(\neg \varphi\) and \(\varphi \wedge \psi\). Hence all quantifier free formulas are absolute.
Finally, if \({}\varphi\) is absolute for \(M\), so is \(\psi \equiv \exists x \in y \: \varphi\): If \(\psi^M(y,\bar{z})\) holds for \(y,\bar{z} \in M\), then we have \([\exists x (x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi(x,y,\bar{z}))]^M\), i.e., \(\exists x \in M(x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z}))\). Since \(\varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z})\) if and only if \(\varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), it follows that \(\exists x\in y \varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), i.e. \({}\psi\).
Conversely, if for \(y,\bar{z} \in M\), \(\exists x\in y \varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), then since \(M\) is transitive, \(x\) belongs to \(M\), and since \(\varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\) if and only \(\varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z})\), we have \(\exists x \in M \, (x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z}) )\) and so \(\psi^M(y,\bar{z})\).











Proposition 2 
Over \(\mathsf{ZF}\), the following properties can be expressed via \(\Delta_0\)-formulas and hence are absolute for any transitive class \(M\):

\(x = \emptyset\), \(x=y\), \(x \subseteq y\), \(z = x \cap y\), \(z = x \cup y\), \(x = \bigcap y\), \(x = \bigcup y\), \(z = \{x,y\}\), \(z =(x,y)\), \(z= x \times y\)
\(r\) is a relation, \(f\) is a function, \(x = \operatorname{dom}(f)\), \(y = \operatorname{ran}(f)\)
\(<\) is a linear order on \(x\), \(x\) is an ordinal, \(x\) is a limit ordinal, \(x=\omega\)





We leave the proof as an exercise.
We can extend the previous absoluteness result to a slightly larger family of formulas.







Definition 3 
A formula \({}\varphi\) is

\(\Sigma_1\) if it is of the form \(\exists x_1 \dots \exists x_m \: \psi\) for a \(\Delta_0\)-formula \(\psi\),
\(\Pi_1\) if it is of the form \(\forall x_1 \dots \forall x_m \: \psi\) for a \(\Delta_0\)-formula \(\psi\).

Given a set of formulas \(T\) and formula \({}\varphi\), we say \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_1^{T}\) if there exists a \(\Sigma_1\)-formula \(\psi_\exists\) and a \(\Pi_1\)-formula \(\psi_\forall\) such that \[
    T \vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi_\exists \quad \text{ and } T \vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi_\forall.
\]











Proposition 3 
If \(M\) is transitive and for all \(\sigma \in T\), \(\sigma^M\) holds, then any \(\Delta_1^T\)-formula is absolute for \(M\)







The absoluteness property of “simple” formulas can be put to use to identify many “almost” models of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) among the levels \(V_\alpha\) of the von Neumann hierarchy. Since each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive, we can check an axiom in \(V_\alpha\) by checking its relativization: all quantifiers range over \(V_\alpha\).
Recall that the rank of a set \(x\) is \[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \min\{\alpha \colon x \in V_{\alpha+1}\}.
\]









Lemma 3 
Each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive.










NoteProof






Proof. By induction on \({}\alpha\). \(V_0 = \emptyset\) is trivially transitive. Suppose \(V_\alpha\) is transitive. We first note that \(V_\alpha \subseteq V_{\alpha+1}\): \[
    z \in V_\alpha \; \overset{V_\alpha \text{ trans.}}{\Longrightarrow} \; z \subseteq V_\alpha \; \Longrightarrow \; z \in \mathcal{P}(V_\alpha) = V_{\alpha+1}.
\] Now \[
    x \in V_{\alpha+1} \; \Rightarrow \; x \in \mathcal{P}(V_\alpha) \; \Rightarrow \; x \subseteq V_\alpha \; \Rightarrow \; x \subseteq V_{\alpha+1}.
\] Limit stages are fine, since a union of transitive sets is transitive.











Lemma 4 
\(x \in V_\omega\) if and only if \(x \subseteq V_\omega\) and \(x\) is finite.










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Since \(V_\omega\) is transitive (Lemma 3), \(x \in V_\omega\) implies \(x \subseteq V_\omega\). Moreover, \(x \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\). By induction on \(n\), each \(V_n\) is finite (\(|V_{n+1}| = 2^{|V_n|}\)), and since \(V_n\) is transitive, \(x \subseteq V_n\), so \(x\) is finite.
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Let \(x \subseteq V_\omega\) be finite. If \(x = \emptyset\), then \(x \in V_1\). Otherwise, each \(y \in x\) has finite rank, so we can let \[
    M = \max\{\operatorname{rank}(y) \colon y \in x\} < \omega.
\] Then \(y \in V_{M+1}\) for all \(y \in x\), i.e. \(x \subseteq V_{M+1}\). Hence \(x \in V_{M+2} \subseteq V_\omega\).




Because of this lemma, the elements of \(V_\omega\) are also called the hereditarily finite sets.







Theorem 2 
\((V_\omega, \in) \models \mathsf{ZF}- \mathsf{Infinity}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We go through the axioms one by one.
Extensionality: The axiom reads \[
    \forall z \, (z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) \to x = y,
\] but in \(V_\omega\) we have to read this as “\(\forall z \in V_\omega\)”. So let \(x,y \in V_\omega\). If \(z \in x \in V_\omega\), then by transitivity \(z \in V_\omega\). So if \(x\) and \(y\) have the same elements in \(V_\omega\), they have the same elements, and thus \(x = y\). In other words, Extensionality follows directly from transitivity.
(Without transitivity, Extensionality can fail: in \(M = \{\emptyset, \mathbb{R}\}\), the sets \(\emptyset \neq \mathbb{R}\) have the same elements in \(M\), namely none. The same happens for \(\{\emptyset, \mathbb{C}\}\).)
Foundation: Every non-empty set has an \(\in\)-minimal element. Let \(x \in V_\omega\), \(x \neq \emptyset\). Choose \(y \in x\) of minimal rank. If \(z \in y\), then \(\operatorname{rank}(z) < \operatorname{rank}(y)\), so \(z \notin x\). Hence \(y\) is \(\in\)-minimal in \(x\) (and \(y \in V_\omega\) by transitivity).
Comprehension: This follows from Lemma 4. Let \(a \in V_\omega\) and let \({}\varphi\) be a formula (possibly with parameters from \(V_\omega\)). Then \[
    z = \{ v \in a \colon \varphi^{V_\omega}(v) \}
\] (\(\varphi\) is evaluated in \(V_\omega\)) is a subset of \(a\). Since \(a \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\), by transitivity \(a \subseteq V_n\), so \(z \subseteq V_n\) and hence \(z \in \mathcal{P}(V_n) = V_{n+1} \subseteq V_\omega\).
Pairing: If \(x, y \in V_\omega\), then \(\{x,y\}\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), hence in \(V_\omega\) by Lemma 4.
Union: Let \(a \in V_\omega\). Then \(\bigcup a\) is a finite union of finite sets and hence finite. Moreover, \[
    \textstyle \bigcup a = \{z \in V_\omega \colon \exists y \in a \; (z \in y)\},
\] since \(a \in V_\omega\) implies, by transitivity, that every \(z \in \bigcup a\) is in \(V_\omega\), i.e. \(\bigcup a \subseteq V_\omega\). By Lemma 4, \(\bigcup a \in V_\omega\).
Power Set: If \(x \in V_\omega\), then \(x \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\), so \(x \subseteq V_n\) and \[
    \mathcal{P}(x) \subseteq \mathcal{P}(V_n) = V_{n+1} \; \Rightarrow \; \mathcal{P}(x) \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(V_n)) = V_{n+2} \subseteq V_\omega.
\] (Alternatively, \(\mathcal{P}(x)\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), so apply Lemma 4.)
Replacement: Suppose \({}\varphi\) defines (in \(V_\omega\)) a function \(f_\varphi: a \to V_\omega\), where \(a \in V_\omega\). Since \(a\) is finite, \(f_\varphi[a]\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), hence, by Lemma 4, \(f_\varphi[a] \in V_\omega\).




On the other hand, Infinity fails in \(V_\omega\), since every element of \(V_\omega\) is finite, while any inductive set is infinite.









TipQuestion



Where are \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\mathbb{C}\), … “located” in the von Neumann hierarchy?









Proposition 4 
For every ordinal \({}\alpha\),

\(\operatorname{rank}(\alpha) = \alpha\),
\(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\cap V_\alpha = \alpha\).





We can represent a rational number as a signed pair of mutually prime natural numbers \(\geq 1\), that is, as \[
    \langle i, \langle m,n \rangle \rangle,
\] where \(i\) codes the sign (with some fixed set representing \(0\)). Each such triple is in \(V_\omega\), by the Pairing argument above. Therefore, \[
    \mathbb{Q}\subseteq V_\omega \quad \leadsto \quad \mathbb{Q}\in V_{\omega+1}.
\]
The real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) are the set of all Dedekind cuts. A Dedekind cut is a subset of \(\mathbb{Q}\), hence an element of \(\mathcal{P}(V_\omega) = V_{\omega+1}\). So all cuts are elements of \(V_{\omega+1}\), i.e. \(\mathbb{R}\subseteq V_{\omega+1}\), and therefore \[
    \mathbb{R}\in V_{\omega+2}.
\]
Finally, \(\mathbb{C}= \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\). An ordered pair \(\langle x,y \rangle = \{\{x\},\{x,y\}\}\) of elements of \(V_{\omega+1}\) is in \(V_{\omega+3}\), so \[
    \mathbb{C}\in V_{\omega+4}.
\]
Continuing like this, it seems that “elementary mathematics” lives in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).






TipQuestion



Which axioms does \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) satisfy?


Replacement fails in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\): The function \(f: n \mapsto \omega + n\) is definable in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) and has domain \(\omega \in V_{\omega+\omega}\). But its range \(\{\omega + n \colon n < \omega\}\) has rank \(\omega+\omega\) (by Proposition 4), so it is not an element of \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).
The other axioms, however, all hold, as the next theorem shows.



Let \(\mathsf{ZC}\) denote \(\mathsf{ZFC}- \mathsf{Replacement}\) (Zermelo set theory with Choice).







Theorem 3 
If \(\alpha > \omega\) is a limit ordinal, then \((V_\alpha, \in) \models \mathsf{ZC}\), i.e. \((V_\alpha, \in) \models \mathsf{ZFC}- \mathsf{Replacement}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We verify a few axioms and leave the rest as an exercise.
Extensionality: The relativized version of this axiom is \[
    \forall a,b \in V_\alpha \, ( \forall x\in V_\alpha (x \in a  \leftrightarrow x \in b)  \to a=b)
\] This simply states that the \(\in\)-relation (as a binary relation) is extensional on \(V_\alpha\) (as defined above). It is easy to see that for every transitive set, the \(\in\)-relation is extensional.
Power Set: We have seen that \(\subseteq\) is absolute for transitive classes. Therefore, the relativized version of the Power Set axiom becomes \[
\forall a \in V_\alpha\, \exists y \in V_\alpha \forall z \in V_\alpha (z \in y \leftrightarrow z \subseteq a)
\] This means we only need to have those subsets in the power set that are in \(V_\alpha\). In other words, we need to verify \[
