\forall a \in V_\alpha\, ( \mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \in V_\alpha)
\] If \(a \in V_\alpha\), then \(a \in V_\beta\) for some \(\beta < \alpha\), since \({}\alpha\) is limit. Since \(V_\beta\) is transitive, \(a \subseteq V_\beta\) and thus \(\mathcal{P}(a)\subseteq \mathcal{P}(V_\beta) = V_{\beta+1}\), which in turn yields \(\mathcal{P}(a) \in V_{\beta+2}\)
If \(b \in \mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha\), then \(b \in V_{\beta+2}\). Therefore, \(\mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \subseteq V_{\beta+2}\). It follows that \(\mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \in V_{\beta+3} \subseteq V_\alpha\), as desired.
Infinity: We have seen that \(x = \omega\) is absolute for transitive classes. Hence \(V_\alpha\) will satisfy the Axiom of Infinity if \(\omega \in V_\alpha\). But this is true since we assume \(\alpha > \omega\).




How about \(V_{\omega_1}\)? Perhaps the failure of Replacement in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) is due to \(\omega+\omega\) being “too small”. But Replacement fails in \(V_{\omega_1}\), too. Consider the formula \[
    \varphi(x,y) \; \iff \; x \subseteq \omega\times\omega \; \wedge \; x \text{ is a well-order} \; \wedge \; y = \operatorname{type}(x).
\] The set \[
    A = \{ x \colon x \subseteq \omega\times\omega, \; x \text{ is a well-order} \}
\] exists in \(V_{\omega_1}\) (it is a subset of \(\mathcal{P}(\omega\times\omega) \subseteq V_{\omega+1}\)). All the relevant notions are absolute for \(V_{\omega_1}\) (for example, the isomorphism between \(x\) and \(\operatorname{type}(x)\) is a subset of \(\omega \times \operatorname{type}(x)\) and hence in \(V_{\omega_1}\)), so \({}\varphi\) defines, in \(V_{\omega_1}\), a function \[
    f: A \to V_{\omega_1}, \quad \operatorname{ran}(f) = \omega_1,
\] since every countable ordinal is the order type of some well-order on a subset of \({}\omega\). But \(\operatorname{rank}(\omega_1) = \omega_1\), so \(\operatorname{ran}(f)\) does not exist in \(V_{\omega_1}\). Hence Replacement fails.
What is the problem with Replacement? The axiom says that if \({}\varphi\) defines a function, then the image of any set under this function is a set. Relativized to some \(M\), this means we need to find a set in \(M\) that contains the image. Here we run into a cardinality problem. The cardinality of \(V_\alpha\) can be much bigger than the cardinality of \({}\alpha\). For example, \(\mathcal{P}(\omega) \in V_{\omega+\omega}\) but \(\omega+\omega\) is countable. We could have a function that maps \(\mathcal{P}(\omega)\) to sets of rank cofinal in \(\omega+\omega\), which implies that the image cannot be in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).
For \(V_\alpha\) to be a model, we would need \({}\alpha\) to be “unreachable” by such mappings. This gives rise to the notion of inaccessible cardinals, which we will introduce in the next section.

title: Models of Set Theory
text:
If we restrict ourselves to models on which the \(E\)-relation is actually well-founded (i.e. from the outside), then interestingly these models look, in a way, “natural”: They can be assumed to be the \(\in\)-relation on a set. Such models are also called standard.
Given a set theoretic structure \((M,E)\) (not necessarily a model of \(\mathsf{ZF}\)), for each \(x \in M\) let \[\begin{equation*}
    \operatorname{ext}_E(x) = \{ y \in X \colon y\, E \, x \}
\end{equation*}\]
If \(E\) behaves “set-like”, then it will respect the axiom of Extensionality, i.e. two sets are identical if and only if they have the same elements. Therefore we say that \(E\) is extensional if \[\begin{equation*}
    x,z \in X, \; x\neq z \quad \text{ implies } \quad \operatorname{ext}_E(x) \neq \operatorname{ext}_E(z).
\end{equation*}\]
Furthermore, as stated above, we want to exclude infinite descending \(E\)-chains. Recall we say that \(E\) is well-founded if

every non-empty set \(Y \subseteq X\) has an \(E\)-minimal element.








Theorem 1 (Mostowski collapse) 
If \(E\) is an extensional and well-founded relation on a set \(X\), then there exists a transitive set \(S\) and a bijection \(\pi: X \to S\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    x \, E \, y \iff \pi(x) \in \pi(y) \quad \text{ for all $ x,y \in X$}.      
\end{equation*}\] Moreover, \(S\) and \({}\pi\) are unique.










NoteProof






Proof. We construct \({}\pi\) and \(S = \operatorname{im}(\pi)\) by recursion on \(E\), which is possible since it is well-founded.
For each \(x \in X\), let \[\begin{equation*}
    \pi(x) = \{\pi(y) \colon y \, E \, x \},
\end{equation*}\] and set \(S = \operatorname{ran}(\pi)\).
The injectivity of \({}\pi\) follows from the extensionality of \({}\pi\) by induction along \(E\):
Suppose we have shown \[\begin{equation*}
\forall z \; (z E x \to \forall y  \in X (\pi(z) = \pi(y) \to z = y)).
\end{equation*}\] and we have to show that it holds for \(x\). Assume \(\pi(x) = \pi(y)\) for some \(y \in X\). Then \[\begin{align*}
cEx &\Rightarrow& \pi(c) \in \pi(x) = \pi(y) &\\
&\Rightarrow& \pi(c) = \pi(z) & \qquad \text{ for some } zEy\\
&\Rightarrow& c=z & \qquad  (\text{by ind. hyp., since } cEx)\\
&\Rightarrow& cEy &.
\end{align*}\] Similarly, we get \(cEy \Rightarrow cEx\), hence \(x=y\) as desired due to the extensionality of \(E\). Finally we have \[\begin{align*}
\pi(x) \in \pi(y) & \Rightarrow & \pi(x) = \pi(c) & \qquad \text{ for some } cEy \\
&\Rightarrow& x = c & \qquad \text{ (since ${}\pi$ is injective)}\\
&\Rightarrow& xEy &
\end{align*}\] Thus \({}\pi\) is an isomorphism.
To see the uniqueness of \({}\pi\) and \(S\), assume \(\rho\), \(T\) are such that the statement of the theorem is satisfied. Then \(\pi \circ \rho^{-1}\) is an isomorphism between \((T, \in)\) and \((S,\in)\). Now apply the following lemma.











Lemma 1 
Suppose \(X,Y\) are sets, and \({}\theta\) is an isomorphism between \((X,\in)\) and \((Y,\in)\). Then \(X=Y\) and \(\theta(x) = x\) for all \(x \in X\).










NoteProof






Proof. By induction on the well-founded relation \(\in\). Assume that \(\theta(z)=z\) for all \(z \in x\) and let \(y = \theta(x)\).
We have \(x \subseteq y\) because if \(z \in x\), then \(z = \theta(z) \in \theta(x) = y\).
We also have \(y \subseteq x\): Let \(t \in y\). Since \(y \in Y\), there is \(z \in X\) with \(\theta(z) = t\). Since \(\theta(z) \in y\) and \(y = \theta(x)\), we have \(z \in x\), and thus \(t = \theta(z) = z \in x\).
Hence \(x = y\), and this also implies \(\theta(x) = x\).











Corollary 1 
If \(E\) is a well-order on a set \(X\), then \((X,E)\) is isomorphic to \((\alpha, \in)\) for a unique ordinal \(\alpha\).










NoteProof






Proof. Every linear order is extensional. Hence we can apply the Mostowski Collapse. It is easy to see that the resulting set is an ordinal.

title: Models of Set Theory
text:
Even if we consider well-founded standard models, interpreting set-theoretic statements in them can still lead to very different results, even for very simple formulas.







Example 1 
Consider \(M = \{0, \{\{0\}\}\}\) and let \(\varphi \equiv \{\{0\}\} \subseteq 0\). Clearly \({}\varphi\) is not true from the “outside”. But what if we look at it from “inside” \(M\)? \(x \subseteq y\) means \(\forall z (z \in x \to z \in y)\). Inside \(M\) this means every set \(z\) in \(M\) that is an element of \(x\) is also an element of \(y\). But in \(M\), there is no element \(z \in \{\{0\}\}\), \(\{0\}\) is not an element of \(M\). Therefore, \[
    (M, \in) \models \{\{0\}\} \subseteq 0.
\]




In the example above, the set \(M\) is not transitive, which allowed it to “hide” its elements. It turns out that if we require our model to be transitive, the truth of simple formulas cannot vary between the “inside” and the “outside” perspective. We call such properties absolute.
Given a formula \({}\varphi\) and some class \(M\), we can relativize \({}\varphi\) with respect to \(M\) essentially by restricting all quantifiers in \({}\varphi\) to range over \(M\), i.e. \(\exists x\) becomes \(\exists x \in M\) and \(\forall x\) becomes \(\forall x \in M\). Note that classes are defined by formulas, so the resulting formula, which we denote by \(\varphi^M\), is still a formula of set theory.







Definition 1 
We say a formula \(\varphi(x_0, \ldots, x_n)\) is absolute for a class \(M\) if for all \(a_0, \ldots, a_n \in M\) \[
    \varphi^M(a_0, \ldots, a_n) \text{ holds} \iff  \varphi(a_0, \ldots, a_n) \text{ holds}.
\]











Exercise 1 If \(M\) is transitive, then for all \({}\varphi\), \[
    (M, \in) \models \varphi \; \iff \; \varphi^M \text{ holds}.
\]











Definition 2 
A formula \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_0\) if it has no quantifiers or every quantifier of \({}\varphi\) is of the form \(\exists x \in y\) or \(\forall x \in y\) (i.e. every quantifier is bounded).











Lemma 2 
If \(M\) is transitive and \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_0\), then \({}\varphi\) is absolute for \(M\).










NoteProof






Proof. Clearly \(x=y\) and \(x\in y\) are absolute for any \(M\). It is also not hard to see that if \({}\varphi\) and \({}\psi\) are absolute for \(M\), then so are \(\neg \varphi\) and \(\varphi \wedge \psi\). Hence all quantifier free formulas are absolute.
Finally, if \({}\varphi\) is absolute for \(M\), so is \(\psi \equiv \exists x \in y \: \varphi\): If \(\psi^M(y,\bar{z})\) holds for \(y,\bar{z} \in M\), then we have \([\exists x (x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi(x,y,\bar{z}))]^M\), i.e., \(\exists x \in M(x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z}))\). Since \(\varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z})\) if and only if \(\varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), it follows that \(\exists x\in y \varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), i.e. \({}\psi\).
Conversely, if for \(y,\bar{z} \in M\), \(\exists x\in y \varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\), then since \(M\) is transitive, \(x\) belongs to \(M\), and since \(\varphi(x,y,\bar{z})\) if and only \(\varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z})\), we have \(\exists x \in M \, (x \in y \: \wedge \: \varphi^M(x,y,\bar{z}) )\) and so \(\psi^M(y,\bar{z})\).











Proposition 2 
Over \(\mathsf{ZF}\), the following properties can be expressed via \(\Delta_0\)-formulas and hence are absolute for any transitive class \(M\):

\(x = \emptyset\), \(x=y\), \(x \subseteq y\), \(z = x \cap y\), \(z = x \cup y\), \(x = \bigcap y\), \(x = \bigcup y\), \(z = \{x,y\}\), \(z =(x,y)\), \(z= x \times y\)
\(r\) is a relation, \(f\) is a function, \(x = \operatorname{dom}(f)\), \(y = \operatorname{ran}(f)\)
\(<\) is a linear order on \(x\), \(x\) is an ordinal, \(x\) is a limit ordinal, \(x=\omega\)





We leave the proof as an exercise.
We can extend the previous absoluteness result to a slightly larger family of formulas.







Definition 3 
A formula \({}\varphi\) is

\(\Sigma_1\) if it is of the form \(\exists x_1 \dots \exists x_m \: \psi\) for a \(\Delta_0\)-formula \(\psi\),
\(\Pi_1\) if it is of the form \(\forall x_1 \dots \forall x_m \: \psi\) for a \(\Delta_0\)-formula \(\psi\).

Given a set of formulas \(T\) and formula \({}\varphi\), we say \({}\varphi\) is \(\Delta_1^{T}\) if there exists a \(\Sigma_1\)-formula \(\psi_\exists\) and a \(\Pi_1\)-formula \(\psi_\forall\) such that \[
    T \vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi_\exists \quad \text{ and } T \vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi_\forall.
\]











Proposition 3 
If \(M\) is transitive and for all \(\sigma \in T\), \(\sigma^M\) holds, then any \(\Delta_1^T\)-formula is absolute for \(M\)

title: Models of Set Theory
text:
The absoluteness property of “simple” formulas can be put to use to identify many “almost” models of \(\mathsf{ZF}\) among the levels \(V_\alpha\) of the von Neumann hierarchy. Since each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive, we can check an axiom in \(V_\alpha\) by checking its relativization: all quantifiers range over \(V_\alpha\).
Recall that the rank of a set \(x\) is \[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \min\{\alpha \colon x \in V_{\alpha+1}\}.
\]









Lemma 3 
Each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive.










NoteProof






Proof. By induction on \({}\alpha\). \(V_0 = \emptyset\) is trivially transitive. Suppose \(V_\alpha\) is transitive. We first note that \(V_\alpha \subseteq V_{\alpha+1}\): \[
    z \in V_\alpha \; \overset{V_\alpha \text{ trans.}}{\Longrightarrow} \; z \subseteq V_\alpha \; \Longrightarrow \; z \in \mathcal{P}(V_\alpha) = V_{\alpha+1}.
\] Now \[
    x \in V_{\alpha+1} \; \Rightarrow \; x \in \mathcal{P}(V_\alpha) \; \Rightarrow \; x \subseteq V_\alpha \; \Rightarrow \; x \subseteq V_{\alpha+1}.
\] Limit stages are fine, since a union of transitive sets is transitive.











Lemma 4 
\(x \in V_\omega\) if and only if \(x \subseteq V_\omega\) and \(x\) is finite.










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Since \(V_\omega\) is transitive (Lemma 3), \(x \in V_\omega\) implies \(x \subseteq V_\omega\). Moreover, \(x \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\). By induction on \(n\), each \(V_n\) is finite (\(|V_{n+1}| = 2^{|V_n|}\)), and since \(V_n\) is transitive, \(x \subseteq V_n\), so \(x\) is finite.
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Let \(x \subseteq V_\omega\) be finite. If \(x = \emptyset\), then \(x \in V_1\). Otherwise, each \(y \in x\) has finite rank, so we can let \[
    M = \max\{\operatorname{rank}(y) \colon y \in x\} < \omega.
\] Then \(y \in V_{M+1}\) for all \(y \in x\), i.e. \(x \subseteq V_{M+1}\). Hence \(x \in V_{M+2} \subseteq V_\omega\).




Because of this lemma, the elements of \(V_\omega\) are also called the hereditarily finite sets.







Theorem 2 
\((V_\omega, \in) \models \mathsf{ZF}- \mathsf{Infinity}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We go through the axioms one by one.
Extensionality: The axiom reads \[
    \forall z \, (z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) \to x = y,
\] but in \(V_\omega\) we have to read this as “\(\forall z \in V_\omega\)”. So let \(x,y \in V_\omega\). If \(z \in x \in V_\omega\), then by transitivity \(z \in V_\omega\). So if \(x\) and \(y\) have the same elements in \(V_\omega\), they have the same elements, and thus \(x = y\). In other words, Extensionality follows directly from transitivity.
(Without transitivity, Extensionality can fail: in \(M = \{\emptyset, \mathbb{R}\}\), the sets \(\emptyset \neq \mathbb{R}\) have the same elements in \(M\), namely none. The same happens for \(\{\emptyset, \mathbb{C}\}\).)
Foundation: Every non-empty set has an \(\in\)-minimal element. Let \(x \in V_\omega\), \(x \neq \emptyset\). Choose \(y \in x\) of minimal rank. If \(z \in y\), then \(\operatorname{rank}(z) < \operatorname{rank}(y)\), so \(z \notin x\). Hence \(y\) is \(\in\)-minimal in \(x\) (and \(y \in V_\omega\) by transitivity).
Comprehension: This follows from Lemma 4. Let \(a \in V_\omega\) and let \({}\varphi\) be a formula (possibly with parameters from \(V_\omega\)). Then \[
    z = \{ v \in a \colon \varphi^{V_\omega}(v) \}
\] (\(\varphi\) is evaluated in \(V_\omega\)) is a subset of \(a\). Since \(a \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\), by transitivity \(a \subseteq V_n\), so \(z \subseteq V_n\) and hence \(z \in \mathcal{P}(V_n) = V_{n+1} \subseteq V_\omega\).
Pairing: If \(x, y \in V_\omega\), then \(\{x,y\}\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), hence in \(V_\omega\) by Lemma 4.
Union: Let \(a \in V_\omega\). Then \(\bigcup a\) is a finite union of finite sets and hence finite. Moreover, \[
    \textstyle \bigcup a = \{z \in V_\omega \colon \exists y \in a \; (z \in y)\},
\] since \(a \in V_\omega\) implies, by transitivity, that every \(z \in \bigcup a\) is in \(V_\omega\), i.e. \(\bigcup a \subseteq V_\omega\). By Lemma 4, \(\bigcup a \in V_\omega\).
Power Set: If \(x \in V_\omega\), then \(x \in V_n\) for some \(n < \omega\), so \(x \subseteq V_n\) and \[
    \mathcal{P}(x) \subseteq \mathcal{P}(V_n) = V_{n+1} \; \Rightarrow \; \mathcal{P}(x) \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(V_n)) = V_{n+2} \subseteq V_\omega.
\] (Alternatively, \(\mathcal{P}(x)\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), so apply Lemma 4.)
Replacement: Suppose \({}\varphi\) defines (in \(V_\omega\)) a function \(f_\varphi: a \to V_\omega\), where \(a \in V_\omega\). Since \(a\) is finite, \(f_\varphi[a]\) is a finite subset of \(V_\omega\), hence, by Lemma 4, \(f_\varphi[a] \in V_\omega\).




On the other hand, Infinity fails in \(V_\omega\), since every element of \(V_\omega\) is finite, while any inductive set is infinite.









TipQuestion



Where are \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\mathbb{C}\), … “located” in the von Neumann hierarchy?









Proposition 4 
For every ordinal \({}\alpha\),

\(\operatorname{rank}(\alpha) = \alpha\),
\(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\cap V_\alpha = \alpha\).





We can represent a rational number as a signed pair of mutually prime natural numbers \(\geq 1\), that is, as \[
    \langle i, \langle m,n \rangle \rangle,
\] where \(i\) codes the sign (with some fixed set representing \(0\)). Each such triple is in \(V_\omega\), by the Pairing argument above. Therefore, \[
    \mathbb{Q}\subseteq V_\omega \quad \leadsto \quad \mathbb{Q}\in V_{\omega+1}.
\]
The real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) are the set of all Dedekind cuts. A Dedekind cut is a subset of \(\mathbb{Q}\), hence an element of \(\mathcal{P}(V_\omega) = V_{\omega+1}\). So all cuts are elements of \(V_{\omega+1}\), i.e. \(\mathbb{R}\subseteq V_{\omega+1}\), and therefore \[
    \mathbb{R}\in V_{\omega+2}.
\]
Finally, \(\mathbb{C}= \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\). An ordered pair \(\langle x,y \rangle = \{\{x\},\{x,y\}\}\) of elements of \(V_{\omega+1}\) is in \(V_{\omega+3}\), so \[
    \mathbb{C}\in V_{\omega+4}.
\]
Continuing like this, it seems that “elementary mathematics” lives in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).






TipQuestion



Which axioms does \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) satisfy?


Replacement fails in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\): The function \(f: n \mapsto \omega + n\) is definable in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) and has domain \(\omega \in V_{\omega+\omega}\). But its range \(\{\omega + n \colon n < \omega\}\) has rank \(\omega+\omega\) (by Proposition 4), so it is not an element of \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).
The other axioms, however, all hold, as the next theorem shows.



Let \(\mathsf{ZC}\) denote \(\mathsf{ZFC}- \mathsf{Replacement}\) (Zermelo set theory with Choice).







Theorem 3 
If \(\alpha > \omega\) is a limit ordinal, then \((V_\alpha, \in) \models \mathsf{ZC}\), i.e. \((V_\alpha, \in) \models \mathsf{ZFC}- \mathsf{Replacement}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We verify a few axioms and leave the rest as an exercise.
Extensionality: The relativized version of this axiom is \[
    \forall a,b \in V_\alpha \, ( \forall x\in V_\alpha (x \in a  \leftrightarrow x \in b)  \to a=b)
\] This simply states that the \(\in\)-relation (as a binary relation) is extensional on \(V_\alpha\) (as defined above). It is easy to see that for every transitive set, the \(\in\)-relation is extensional.
Power Set: We have seen that \(\subseteq\) is absolute for transitive classes. Therefore, the relativized version of the Power Set axiom becomes \[
\forall a \in V_\alpha\, \exists y \in V_\alpha \forall z \in V_\alpha (z \in y \leftrightarrow z \subseteq a)
\] This means we only need to have those subsets in the power set that are in \(V_\alpha\). In other words, we need to verify \[
\forall a \in V_\alpha\, ( \mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \in V_\alpha)
\] If \(a \in V_\alpha\), then \(a \in V_\beta\) for some \(\beta < \alpha\), since \({}\alpha\) is limit. Since \(V_\beta\) is transitive, \(a \subseteq V_\beta\) and thus \(\mathcal{P}(a)\subseteq \mathcal{P}(V_\beta) = V_{\beta+1}\), which in turn yields \(\mathcal{P}(a) \in V_{\beta+2}\)
If \(b \in \mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha\), then \(b \in V_{\beta+2}\). Therefore, \(\mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \subseteq V_{\beta+2}\). It follows that \(\mathcal{P}(a) \cap V_\alpha \in V_{\beta+3} \subseteq V_\alpha\), as desired.
Infinity: We have seen that \(x = \omega\) is absolute for transitive classes. Hence \(V_\alpha\) will satisfy the Axiom of Infinity if \(\omega \in V_\alpha\). But this is true since we assume \(\alpha > \omega\).




How about \(V_{\omega_1}\)? Perhaps the failure of Replacement in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\) is due to \(\omega+\omega\) being “too small”. But Replacement fails in \(V_{\omega_1}\), too. Consider the formula \[
    \varphi(x,y) \; \iff \; x \subseteq \omega\times\omega \; \wedge \; x \text{ is a well-order} \; \wedge \; y = \operatorname{type}(x).
\] The set \[
    A = \{ x \colon x \subseteq \omega\times\omega, \; x \text{ is a well-order} \}
\] exists in \(V_{\omega_1}\) (it is a subset of \(\mathcal{P}(\omega\times\omega) \subseteq V_{\omega+1}\)). All the relevant notions are absolute for \(V_{\omega_1}\) (for example, the isomorphism between \(x\) and \(\operatorname{type}(x)\) is a subset of \(\omega \times \operatorname{type}(x)\) and hence in \(V_{\omega_1}\)), so \({}\varphi\) defines, in \(V_{\omega_1}\), a function \[
    f: A \to V_{\omega_1}, \quad \operatorname{ran}(f) = \omega_1,
\] since every countable ordinal is the order type of some well-order on a subset of \({}\omega\). But \(\operatorname{rank}(\omega_1) = \omega_1\), so \(\operatorname{ran}(f)\) does not exist in \(V_{\omega_1}\). Hence Replacement fails.
What is the problem with Replacement? The axiom says that if \({}\varphi\) defines a function, then the image of any set under this function is a set. Relativized to some \(M\), this means we need to find a set in \(M\) that contains the image. Here we run into a cardinality problem. The cardinality of \(V_\alpha\) can be much bigger than the cardinality of \({}\alpha\). For example, \(\mathcal{P}(\omega) \in V_{\omega+\omega}\) but \(\omega+\omega\) is countable. We could have a function that maps \(\mathcal{P}(\omega)\) to sets of rank cofinal in \(\omega+\omega\), which implies that the image cannot be in \(V_{\omega+\omega}\).
For \(V_\alpha\) to be a model, we would need \({}\alpha\) to be “unreachable” by such mappings. This gives rise to the notion of inaccessible cardinals, which we will introduce in the next section.

title: Ordinals
text: We work in ZFC, but — as noted below — we deliberately avoid using Foundation, so that “being an ordinal” does real work.

title: Ordinals
text:
Why count past \(\mathbb{N}\)?
Cantor was led to the transfinite by a concrete problem. Given \(A \subseteq
\mathbb{R}\), its derivative is the set of its limit points,
\[
A' = \{\, x \in A : x \text{ is a limit point of } A \,\}.
\]
Iterating gives a descending chain \(A \supseteq A' \supseteq A'' \supseteq
\cdots\), and one can take a “limit” \(A^{(\infty)} = \bigcap_n A^{(n)}\). But \(A^{(\infty)}\) may still have isolated points, so the process continues: \(A^{(\infty)} \supsetneq (A^{(\infty)})' \supsetneq \cdots\). To index the stages we need numbers beyond the natural numbers:
\[
0, 1, 2, \dots, \omega, \omega+1, \omega+2, \dots, \omega+\omega, \dots,
\omega\cdot\omega, \dots
\]
Making “keep counting, even through limit stages” precise is exactly what the ordinals accomplish. The concept they rest on is the well-order.

title: Ordinals
text:
Well-founded relations
Throughout, \(R\) is a relation on a set \(A\), and for \(X \subseteq A\) we write \(R\restriction X = \{\langle x,y\rangle \in R : x, y \in X\}\).


\(y\) is \(R\)-minimal in \(X\):

\(y \in X\) and \(\neg\exists z\,(z \in X \wedge z \mathbin{R} y)\) — nothing in \(X\) is \(R\)-below \(y\).

\(R\) is well-founded on \(A\):

every nonempty \(X \subseteq A\) has an \(R\)-minimal element: \[
\forall X\,\bigl(\varnothing \neq X \subseteq A \;\rightarrow\;
\exists y \in X\;\forall z \in X\;\neg(z \mathbin{R} y)\bigr).
\]



Two basic facts:

The Axiom of Foundation says exactly that \(\in\) is well-founded on every set. We will not assume this below.
If \(A\) is finite, then \(R\) is well-founded on \(A\) iff \(R\) has no cycles \(a_0 \mathbin{R} a_1 \mathbin{R} \cdots \mathbin{R} a_n \mathbin{R} a_0\) on \(A\). (For infinite \(A\) this fails: the usual \(<\) on \(\mathbb{Q}\) is acyclic but not well-founded.)

Well-foundedness is the “no infinite descent” condition; it is what makes proof by induction and definition by recursion possible.

title: Ordinals
text:
Well-orders


Definition. \(R\) is a well-order (WO) on \(A\):

\(R\) totally orders \(A\) strictly and \(R\) is well-founded on \(A\).



Equivalently: a strict total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element. (In a total order an \(R\)-minimal element of \(X\) is automatically the \(R\)-least element of \(X\).)
Examples.

\((\mathbb{N}, <)\) is a well-order — this is the least number principle.
\(\bigl(\{\,1 - 2^{-n} : n \in \mathbb{N}\,\},\,<\bigr)\) is a well-order.
\(\bigl(\{\,m - 2^{-n} : m, n \geq 1\,\},\,<\bigr)\) is a well-order (a copy of \(\mathbb{N}\) followed by another copy, then another, …).
\((\mathbb{Q}, <)\), \((\mathbb{R}, <)\), \((\mathbb{Z}, <)\) are not WOs.


Well-orders are rigid
Orders are compared by embeddings: \(f : (A, <_A) \to (B, <_B)\) with \(x <_A y \leftrightarrow f(x) <_B f(y)\). An isomorphism is a bijective embedding; \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{R}\) have nontrivial automorphisms (\(z \mapsto
z+1\)). Well-orders do not.

Proposition. Let \((A, <)\) be a well-order and \(f : A \to A\) a self-embedding. Then \(x \leq f(x)\) for all \(x \in A\).

Proof. If \(\{x \in A : f(x) < x\} \neq \varnothing\), it has a least element \(z\). Then \(f(z) < z\), and applying the embedding \(f\bigl(f(z)\bigr) < f(z)\) — so \(f(z)\) is a smaller element of the set, contradicting minimality of \(z\). \(\square\)

Corollary. The only automorphism of a well-order is the identity.

Proof. If \(f\) is an automorphism, both \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) are self-embeddings, so \(x \leq f(x)\) and \(x \leq f^{-1}(x)\); the latter gives \(f(x) \leq x\). \(\square\)
For \(b \in A\), the initial segment below \(b\) is
\[
A_{<b} \;:=\; \{\, a \in A : a < b \,\}.
\]

Corollary. No well-order is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of itself.

Proof. Suppose \(f : A \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } A_{<b}\). Then \(f(x) < b\) for every \(x\), in particular \(f(b) < b\) — contradicting the Proposition. \(\square\)

title: Ordinals
text:
Ordinal numbers
Cantor defined an ordinal as an isomorphism class of well-orders (an “order type”). von Neumann gave a canonical representative of each class: a specific set on which \(\in\) is the ordering. For instance
\[
3 = \bigl\{\, \varnothing,\ \{\varnothing\},\ \{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}
\,\bigr\}
\]
is a \(3\)-element set well-ordered by \(\in\).


Definition. A set \(A\) is transitive:

\(\forall x \in A\;(x \subseteq A)\) — every element is also a subset. (A transitive set cannot “hide” members inside its members.)

Definition (von Neumann). A set \(z\) is an ordinal, \(\operatorname{Ord}(z)\):

\(z\) is transitive and well-ordered by \(\in\).




We do not assume Foundation here. If we did, “well-ordered by \(\in\)” could be weakened to “linearly ordered by \(\in\)”, since well-foundedness would come for free. 



Proposition 1. If \(\operatorname{Ord}(\alpha)\) and \(x \in \alpha\), then \(\operatorname{Ord}(x)\). (Every element of an ordinal is an ordinal.)

Proof. Since \(\alpha\) is transitive, \(x \subseteq \alpha\), so \(\in\) well-orders \(x\) (a subset of a well-order is well-ordered). It remains to show \(x\) is a transitive set. Let \(y \in z \in x\). Then \(z \in \alpha\) (as \(x \subseteq
\alpha\)), so \(y \in \alpha\) (as \(z \subseteq \alpha\)). Now \(x, y \in \alpha\) and \(\in\) is a total order on \(\alpha\), so
\[
y \in x \quad\vee\quad x \in y \quad\vee\quad x = y.
\]
If \(x = y\) then \(x \in z \in x\); if \(x \in y\) then \(x \in y \in z \in x\) — both are \(\in\)-cycles in \(\alpha\), impossible since \(\in\) is well-founded on \(\alpha\). Hence \(y \in x\). \(\square\)
This suggests ordering ordinals by
\[
\alpha < \beta \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad \alpha \in \beta,
\]
and Proposition 1 gives, for every ordinal,
\[
\alpha \;=\; \{\, \beta : \beta < \alpha \,\}
\]
— an ordinal is the set of all smaller ordinals.

title: Ordinals
text:
The well-ordering of the ordinals

Proposition 2. For ordinals \(\alpha, \beta\): \(\quad\alpha < \beta \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \alpha \subsetneq \beta\).

Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) \(\alpha \in \beta\) and \(\beta\) transitive give \(\alpha
\subseteq \beta\); properly, since \(\alpha \notin \alpha\) (well-foundedness) while \(\alpha \in \beta\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) We prove the stronger statement
\[
\operatorname{trans}(a) \;\wedge\; a \subsetneq \beta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{Ord}(a) \;\wedge\; a \in \beta.
\]
If \(a \subsetneq \beta\) then \(a\) is linearly ordered by \(\in\) (subset of \(\beta\)); being also transitive, \(a\) is an ordinal. For \(a \in \beta\): since \(\beta
\setminus a \neq \varnothing\), pick \(\gamma\) \(\in\)-minimal in \(\beta \setminus a\). We claim \(\gamma = a\).

\(\gamma \subseteq a\): if \(g \in \gamma\) then \(g \notin \beta \setminus a\) by minimality, and \(g \in \beta\) (transitivity of \(\beta\)), so \(g \in a\).
\(a \subseteq \gamma\): let \(x \in a\). Then \(x \in \beta\), so by trichotomy in \(\beta\), \(x \in \gamma \vee \gamma \in x \vee x = \gamma\). The last two force \(\gamma \in a\) (transitivity of \(a\), resp. directly), contradicting \(\gamma
\notin a\). So \(x \in \gamma\).

Hence \(a = \gamma \in \beta\). \(\square\)
Write \(ON = \{\, x : \operatorname{Ord}(x) \,\}\) for the collection of all ordinals.

Theorem. \(ON\) is well-ordered by \(<\) (\(=\in\)).
Since \(ON\) is not a set (next result), this is shorthand for a list of ZFC theorems: \(\in\) on the ordinals is (1) transitive, (2) irreflexive, (3) trichotomous, and (4) well-founded — every nonempty set of ordinals has an \(\in\)-least member.

Proof.

Transitive: \(\alpha < \beta < \gamma\) means \(\alpha \in \beta \in \gamma\); \(\gamma\) transitive gives \(\alpha \in \gamma\).
Irreflexive: \(\alpha \in \alpha\) would be an \(\in\)-cycle in \(\alpha\), contradicting well-foundedness of \(\in\) on \(\alpha\).
Trichotomy: first a lemma.

Lemma. \(\alpha \cap \beta\) is an ordinal.
It is transitive (an intersection of transitive sets is transitive) and well-ordered by \(\in\) (a subset of \(\alpha\)).

Let \(\gamma = \alpha \cap \beta\), so \(\gamma \subseteq \alpha\) and \(\gamma
\subseteq \beta\). By Proposition 2, \(\gamma \in \alpha\) or \(\gamma = \alpha\), and likewise for \(\beta\). If \(\gamma \in \alpha\) and \(\gamma \in \beta\) then \(\gamma \in \alpha \cap \beta = \gamma\), impossible. So \(\gamma = \alpha\) or \(\gamma = \beta\); that is \(\alpha \subseteq \beta\) or \(\beta \subseteq \alpha\), hence (Proposition 2) \(\alpha \leq \beta\) or \(\beta \leq \alpha\).
Well-founded: let \(A \neq \varnothing\) be a set of ordinals and \(\alpha \in
A\). If \(\alpha\) is \(\in\)-least, done. Otherwise \(\alpha \cap A = \{\beta \in A
: \beta < \alpha\}\) is a nonempty subset of \(\alpha\), so it has an \(\in\)-least element (since \(\in\) well-orders \(\alpha\)) — and that is \(\in\)-least in \(A\). \(\square\)


Burali-Forti. \(ON\) is a proper class: no set contains all the ordinals.

Proof. If every ordinal were in a set \(X\), then \(ON = \{y \in X :
\operatorname{Ord}(y)\}\) would be a set. It is transitive (Proposition 1) and well-ordered by \(\in\) (Theorem), hence an ordinal, hence \(ON \in ON\) — contradicting irreflexivity. (This needs no Foundation: ordinals are by definition strictly ordered by \(\in\).) \(\square\)
Working in Cantor’s naive set theory, Burali-Forti (1897) put together “the well-ordering of all well-orderings” to get a well-ordering strictly longer than every well-ordering, including itself.

title: Ordinals
text:
The natural numbers, again
Recall \(\omega\) was introduced (Axiom of Infinity) as the smallest inductive set — the smallest set containing \(\varnothing\) and closed under the successor
\[
S(x) = x \cup \{x\}.
\]

Proposition 3. If \(\operatorname{Ord}(\alpha)\) then \(\operatorname{Ord}\bigl(
S(\alpha)\bigr)\), and for every ordinal \(\gamma\), \(\quad\gamma < S(\alpha) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \gamma \leq \alpha\).

Proof (sketch). \(S(\alpha) = \alpha \cup \{\alpha\}\) is transitive: its members are the members of \(\alpha\) (each \(\subseteq \alpha \subseteq S(\alpha)\)) and \(\alpha\) itself (\(\subseteq S(\alpha)\)). It is well-ordered by \(\in\): it is \(\alpha\) with one new top element. The equivalence is then immediate from \(\gamma \in \alpha \cup \{\alpha\}\). \(\square\)


\(\alpha\) is a successor

\(\alpha = S(\beta)\) for some ordinal \(\beta\).

\(\alpha\) is a limit

\(\alpha \neq 0\) and \(\alpha\) is not a successor. Equivalently: \(\alpha \neq 0\) and \(\forall \beta < \alpha\;(S(\beta) < \alpha)\).

\(\alpha\) is finite (a natural number)

every \(\beta \leq \alpha\) is either \(0\) or a successor.




Proposition 4. If \(\alpha\) is finite, so is \(S(\alpha)\).

Now consider the class \(X = \{\, x : x \text{ is a finite ordinal} \,\}\). It contains \(0\) and is closed under \(S\) (Proposition 4) — it is inductive. Since \(\omega\) is the smallest inductive set, \(\omega \subseteq X\): every element of \(\omega\) is a finite ordinal.
Claim: there is no finite ordinal outside \(\omega\). Suppose \(n \in X
\setminus \omega\). (We cannot apply the least-element principle to \(X \setminus
\omega\) directly — it might be a proper class.) But \(S(n) \setminus \omega\) is a set (a subset of the ordinal \(S(n)\)), nonempty (\(n\) is in it), and consists of finite ordinals. So it has an \(\in\)-least element \(k\).

\(k \neq 0\), since \(0 \in \omega\).
So \(k\) is a successor, \(k = S(j)\). Then \(j \in k\), so by leastness \(j \notin
S(n) \setminus \omega\); but \(j \in S(n)\), so \(j \in \omega\). Since \(\omega\) is closed under \(S\), \(k = S(j) \in \omega\) — contradicting \(k \notin \omega\).

So \(X \setminus \omega = \varnothing\). \(\square\)

Proposition 5. Every set \(X\) that is an initial segment of \(ON\) — i.e. \(\forall \beta \in X\;\forall \alpha < \beta\;(\alpha \in X)\) — is an ordinal.

Proof. \(X\) is well-ordered by \(\in\) (Theorem). The initial-segment condition says \(\alpha \in \beta \in X \Rightarrow \alpha \in X\), i.e. \(X\) is transitive. \(\square\)

Corollary. \(\omega\) is an ordinal.

Proof. By the Claim, \(\omega\) is a set of ordinals; and it is an initial segment of \(ON\) (if \(\beta \in \omega\) and \(\alpha < \beta\) then \(\alpha\) is a finite ordinal, and \(\alpha \in \omega\) because every element of a finite ordinal is a finite ordinal, hence in \(\omega\)). Apply Proposition 5. \(\square\)

Corollary. \(\omega\) is the least limit ordinal.

Proof. \(\omega \neq 0\), and \(\omega\) is not a successor (if \(\omega = S(n)\) then \(n \in \omega\) and \(\omega = S(n) \in \omega\)). So \(\omega\) is a limit. Every smaller ordinal is a finite ordinal, hence \(0\) or a successor — not a limit. \(\square\)
We can keep going:
\[
\omega,\ \ S(\omega) = \omega+1,\ \ \omega+2,\ \dots,\ \
\underbrace{\omega+\omega}_{\omega\cdot 2},\ \dots,\ \omega\cdot\omega,\ \dots,\
\omega^{\omega},\ \dots,\ \omega^{\omega^{\omega}},\ \dots,\ \varepsilon_0,\ \dots
\]
(Ordinal \(+\), \(\cdot\), and exponentiation are defined by transfinite recursion later.) Every ordinal displayed here is still a countable set; the supremum of all countable ordinals is \(\omega_1\), the first uncountable ordinal.

title: Ordinals
text:
Representing well-orders as ordinals
The point of the von Neumann definition: each well-order should have exactly one ordinal representative.
We have already shown, for ordinals:

no ordinal is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of itself;
the only automorphism of an ordinal is the identity.

By trichotomy, (1) gives uniqueness: if \(\alpha \cong \beta\) then \(\alpha =
\beta\). (If \(\alpha < \beta\) then \(\alpha = \beta_{<\alpha}\) is a proper initial segment of \(\beta\), so \(\alpha \cong \beta\) would violate (1).)

Representation Theorem for WOs. If \(R\) well-orders \(A\), then there is a unique ordinal \(\alpha\) with \((A, R) \cong (\alpha, \in)\). The isomorphism is unique.
\(\alpha\) is called the order type of \((A, R)\), written \(\operatorname{type}
(A, R)\).

Proof. Uniqueness of \(\alpha\) is the remark above; uniqueness of the isomorphism follows from (2). For existence:
For \(a \in A\) put \(A_{<a} = \{x \in A : x \mathbin{R} a\}\); it is well-ordered by \(R\). Call \(a\) good if \((A_{<a}, R) \cong (\xi, \in)\) for some ordinal \(\xi\) — by uniqueness this \(\xi\) and the isomorphism \(h_a\) are then determined. Let
\[
G = \{\, a \in A : a \text{ is good} \,\}.
\]
By Replacement, \(f : G \to ON\), \(f(a) =\) the unique ordinal \(\cong (A_{<a}, R)\), is a function.
Observation. For \(a \in G\) and \(c \mathbin{R} a\): \(c \in G\), \(h_c = h_a
\restriction A_{<c}\), and \(f(c) = h_a(c)\). In particular \(G\) is an initial segment of \(A\), and \(f\) is order-preserving: \(a \mathbin{R} b \Rightarrow f(a) =
h_b(a) \in f(b)\), i.e. \(f(a) < f(b)\).
\(\operatorname{ran}(f)\) is an initial segment of \(ON\). If \(\xi = f(a) =
\operatorname{ran}(h_a)\) and \(\eta < \xi\), then \(\eta = h_a(b)\) for some \(b
\mathbin{R} a\), and \(h_a(b) = f(b)\), so \(\eta \in \operatorname{ran}(f)\).
By Proposition 5, \(\alpha := \operatorname{ran}(f)\) is an ordinal, and \(f : G
\xrightarrow{\cong} \alpha\).
Finally \(G = A\). If not, let \(a\) be \(R\)-minimal in \(A \setminus G\). Since \(G\) is an initial segment of \(A\), \(A_{<a} = G\), so \((A_{<a}, R) \cong (\alpha, \in)\) — making \(a\) good, a contradiction. \(\square\)

Looking ahead: transfinite induction
The existence proof quietly used a “least counterexample” argument on a well-order. Its systematic form, valid on \(ON\) itself:

Transfinite Induction. Let \(P\) be a property of ordinals. If

\(P(0)\);
\(P(\alpha) \Rightarrow P\bigl(S(\alpha)\bigr)\) for all \(\alpha\);
for every limit \(\lambda\): \(\bigl(\forall \beta < \lambda\; P(\beta)\bigr)
\Rightarrow P(\lambda)\);

then \(P(\alpha)\) for all ordinals \(\alpha\).

Informally: a least \(\alpha\) with \(\neg P(\alpha)\) would have to be \(0\), a successor, or a limit, and each case is excluded. Turning this — and the matching recursion principle — into theorems (given that \(ON\) is a proper class) is the next topic.

title: The Axiom of Choice
text:
The Axiom of Choice
Can every set be well-ordered? This property is equivalent to the Axiom of Choice and therefore has a somewhat controversial ontological status among mathematicians.
Let \(X\) be a set of non-empty sets. A choice function for \(X\) is a function \(f\) that assigns every set \(Y \in X\) an element \(y \in Y\).






NoteAxiom of Choice (\(\mathsf{AC}\))



Every set \(X\) of non-empty sets has a choice function.


The Axiom of Choice allows for enumerating a (non-empty) set \(A\) by using a choice function for all non-empty subsets of \(A\). If the set of elements of \(A\) not yet enumerated is non-empty, the choice function applied to this set will give us the next element to be enumerated (thereby well-ordering \(A\)). On the other hand, if \(A\) is well-ordered, we can obtain a choice function by mapping a non-empty subset of \(A\) to its least element under the well-ordering.
It follows that the Axiom of Choice is equivalent to Zermelo’s Well-Ordering Principle:






NoteWell-Ordering Principle (\(\mathsf{WO}\))



Every set can be well-ordered


Besides \(\mathsf{WO}\), \(\mathsf{AC}\) has applications in pretty much any branch of mathematics, with many equivalent principles (such as Zorn’s Lemma, that every vector space has a basis, and Tychonoff’s theorem), but also some strange consequences (such as the Banach–Tarski paradox).
The foundational issue with the Axiom of Choice lies primarily in the fact that it postulates the existence of a function without giving any hint at how such a function might be defined. For some sets (e.g., the rationals) we can explicitly describe a well-ordering (by identifying \(\mathbb{Q}\) with a subset of \(\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}\) and then well-ordering that). But \(\mathsf{AC}\) also guarantees a well-order of the reals, and if you try to ‘write down’ such a well-order, you will quickly run into difficulties.







Remark 1 (Further reading). For more on the history and the controversy surrounding the Axiom of Choice, see G.H. Moore: Zermelo’s Axiom of Choice, Springer. 1982.




We will need the Axiom of Choice in many places. In the next section, we will use it to develop the theory of cardinal numbers. Some axioms that are considered in descriptive set theory (such as the Axiom of Determinacy, \(\mathsf{AD}\)) contradict \(\mathsf{AC}\). It is therefore important to keep track of where exactly we use the Axiom of Choice.
For some applications, it suffices to use weaker forms of \(\mathsf{AC}\).






NoteAxiom of Countable Choice (\(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\))



\[
\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\; A_n \ne \emptyset \quad \Rightarrow \quad  \exists f \; \forall n \in \omega \;  f(n) \in A_n
\]








NoteAxiom of Dependent Choice (\(\mathsf{DC}\))



If \(R\) is a binary relation on a set \(A\), \(a_0 \in A\), and \(\forall x \in A \exists y \in A \; xRy\), then \[
\exists f : \mathbb{N}\longrightarrow A  \text{ with }  \; f(0) = a_0  \; \wedge  \;\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\; f(n) R f(n+1).
\]









Proposition 1 
\(\mathsf{AC}\) implies \(\mathsf{DC}\) and \(\mathsf{DC}\) implies \(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\).




Both implications are strict, in the sense that there are mathematical universes in which the weaker axiom holds and the stronger fails.
The axiom \(\mathsf{AC}_{\omega}\) is sufficient to prove, for example, the following:

Every infinite set contains a countably infinite subset.
A countable union of countable sets is countable.

\(\mathsf{DC}\) and \(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\) therefore play an important role in the foundations of analysis and measure theory.

title: Induction and Recursion
text:
While the class \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\) of all ordinals is not a set, it is still transitive and well-ordered by \(\in\). Regarding the associated order \(\leq\), every set of ordinals \(a\) has a supremum \(\bigcup a = \bigcup_{\xi \in a} \xi\) and (if \(a \ne \emptyset\)) an infimum \(\bigcap a = \bigcap_{\xi \in a} \xi\), which is the smallest element of \(a\). Such a smallest element exists actually for every (non-empty) class \(A\) (since if \(\xi \in A\), we only need to find the infimum of the set of ordinals \(\le \xi\).) This allows us to prove properties about all ordinals by induction.







Proposition 1 (Induction for ordinals, I) 
For every property \(\varphi\), \[\begin{equation*}
    \forall \alpha \; [ \forall \xi < \alpha \; \varphi(\xi) \to \varphi(\alpha)] \to \forall \alpha \, \varphi(\alpha).
\end{equation*}\]




We have repeatedly used induction already for ordinals \(< \omega_1\), the first uncountable ordinal.
To prove this principle simply observe that if \(\forall \alpha \, \varphi(\alpha)\) failed there would have to be a smallest \({}\alpha\) with \(\neg \varphi(\alpha)\), contradicting the induction hypothesis.
Since every ordinal is either \(0\), a successor, or a limit ordinal, we have the following variant of induction.







Proposition 2 (Induction for ordinals, II) 
For every property \({}\varphi\), if

(i) \(\varphi(0)\),
(ii) \(\forall \alpha (\varphi(\alpha) \to \varphi(\alpha+1))\), and
(iii) \((\forall \xi < \lambda \; \varphi(\xi)) \to \varphi(\lambda))\) for all limit \(\lambda\),

then \(\forall \alpha \;  \varphi(\alpha)\).




(i) and (ii) coincide with the usual induction scheme for natural numbers. To cover all ordinals we need to add (iii).



The induction principle can be used to define functions by recursion. For example, addition on the natural numbers is given by
\[\begin{align*}
    x+0 \quad & =  x\\
    x+ (y+1) & =  (x + y)+1.
\end{align*}\]
In the case of ordinals, we have to consider the limit case, too.







Theorem 1 (Recursion on ordinals) 
If \(G : \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) is a function, then there exists a unique function \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that for all \(\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\),
\[
F(\alpha) = G(F\mid_{\alpha})
\]










NoteProof






Proof. The uniqueness of the function \(F\) follows by induction.
To show the existence of \(F\), we define the following:

Call \(h\) tame if \[\begin{equation*}
\exists \alpha \, (h: \alpha \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\wedge \forall \xi \in \alpha \; h(\xi) = G(h \mid_{\xi}))
\end{equation*}\]
Say \(h\) is compatible with \(g\) if \[\begin{equation*}
  \forall x \in \operatorname{Dom}(h) \cap \operatorname{Dom}(g) \; h(x) = g(x)
\end{equation*}\]

It follows by induction that any two tame functions are compatible.
This lets us define the desired \(F\) as
\[
F := \bigcup \{h \colon h\, \text{ tame}\}
\]
Then \(F\) is a function (otherwise there would be two incompatible tame functions), its domain is transitive, and satisfies the recursion condition (since it is the union of tame functions).
It remains to show that \(F\) is defined on all of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\). If \(D = \operatorname{Dom}(F) \neq \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\), then we would have \(D = \alpha\) for some ordinal \({}\alpha\). In particular \(D\) is a set therefore \(F = f\) is a set, for some tame \(f\). This \(f\) could be extended to a tame \(h = f \cup \{(\alpha,G(f \mid_{\alpha}))\}\), contradiction.




Note that we defined \(F\) explicitly as a union of all partial solutions to the recursion equation. (Of course, since \(F\) is a proper class, one has the translate the informal definition of \(F\) above into a formal expression.)
As with induction, we have the following variant of the recursion principle.







Proposition 3 (Recursion on ordinals, variant) 
If \(G, H: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) are functions and \(a\) is a set, then there exists a unique function \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{align*}
    F(0) \quad & =  a\\
    F(\alpha+1) & =  G(\alpha,F(\alpha)) \\    
    F(\lambda) \quad & =  H(\lambda, \{F(\xi) \colon \xi<\lambda \}) \quad \text{for } \operatorname{Lim}(\lambda).
\end{align*}\]




We can establish a similar principle for a well-ordering \(<\) on a class \(A\). In case of a proper class, though, we have to require that for every \(a \in A\), the class of all predecessors of \(a\) \[\begin{equation*}
S(a,<): = \{x \in A\colon x < a \},
\end{equation*}\] is a set (if \(A\) is a set, this follows automatically by Separation). If this is the case, the recursion principle yields a function \(F: A \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    F(a) = G(a,F\mid_{S(a,<)}).
\end{equation*}\]



More generally, we can define induction and recursion on well-founded relations. We already encountered those in a previous chapter.







Definition 1 
A relation \(R\) on a class \(A\) is well-founded if it satisfies the minimality condition \[\begin{equation*}
    (\operatorname{Min}_R) \qquad  \emptyset \neq b \subset A \to \exists x \in b \; \forall y \in b \, (  \neg y R x)
\end{equation*}\] and the set condition \[\begin{equation*}
    \forall x \in A \; S(a,R):= \{x \colon x R a\} \text{ is a set}
\end{equation*}\]




If \(A\) is a set, the minimality condition is again automatically satisfied by Separation.
The set condition allows for taking the \(R\)-transitive closure of a set \(a \in A\): the smallest superset \(\operatorname{TC}_R(a)\) of \(a\) that is \(R\)-transitive:
\[ \forall x \in \operatorname{TC}_R(a)\; S(x,R) \subseteq  \operatorname{TC}_R(a)\]
This is done by recursion over the natural numbers. The following is an important example.







Example 1 (Transitive closure of a set) 
By the axiom of Foundation, \(\in\) is a well-founded relation on \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\). (The set condition is satisfied since \(S(a,\in)=a\).)
We can form the transitive closure, the smallest transitive superset, of a set \(a\) as
\[\begin{align*}
    \operatorname{TC}(a):&= a \cup \bigcup a \cup \bigcup \bigcup a \ldots
= \bigcup_{n< \omega} U^n(a), \quad \text{ where} \\
&U^0(a) = a, U^{n+1}(a) = \bigcup U^n(a).
\end{align*}\]
This is an example of definition by recursion along \(\mathbb{N}\).




We can use the existence of \(\operatorname{TC}_R\) as a set to strengthen the minimality condition to subclasses, similar to the case of the well-ordering of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\):







Lemma 1 
For every non-empty class \(B \subseteq A\), there exists \(x \in B\) such that
\[
    \forall y \in B \;  \neg y R x
\]




To prove this lemma, simply pick any \(x \in B\), take its transitive \(R\)-closure, and intersect it with \(B\):
\[
    C = \operatorname{TC}_R(x) \cap B.
\]
\(C\) is a set, and by the minimality condition \((\operatorname{Min}_R)\) has an \(R\)-minimal element \(a\). \(a\) has to be minimal for \(B\), too, since otherwise there exists \(b \in B\) with \(b R a\). Since \(a \in \operatorname{TC}_R(x)\), \(b \in \operatorname{TC}_R(x)\), and therefore \(b \in C\), contradicting the minimality of \(a\).
The lemma implies a corresponding induction principle for well-founded relations:
\[\begin{equation*}
    (\operatorname{Ind}_R) \qquad  \forall x \in A [ \forall y ( yRx \, \to \varphi(y)) \to \varphi(x)] \to \forall x \in A \, \varphi(x)).
\end{equation*}\]
This in turn yields the following.







Theorem 2 (Recursion principle for well-founded relations) 
Let \(R\) be a well-founded relation on a class \(A\). For every function \(G : A \times \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) there exists a unique function \(F: A \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    F(a) = G(a,F \mid_{\{x \mid xRa\}})  \text{ for all } a \in A.
\end{equation*}\]







Is there a way to systematically build the \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), the universe of all sets, “from below”?
We start with the empty set:
\[
V_0 = \emptyset
\]
Given \(V_\alpha\), the Power Set axiom requires the set of all subsets to exist, so we set
\[
V_{\alpha+1} = \mathcal{P}(V_{\alpha}).
\]
Finally, at limit stages we simply collect all sets we have obtained so far:
\[
V_ \lambda =  \bigcup_{\xi < \lambda} V_\xi \quad \text{for limit } \lambda
\]
What we really are doing here is to construct a function \(V: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) by ordinal recursion. Think \(V_\alpha = V(\alpha)\).
The following facts about the hierarchy are easily verified by transfinite induction:







Proposition 4  

Each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive.
\(\alpha < \beta\) implies \(V_\alpha \subset V_\beta\).
\(\alpha \subseteq V_\alpha\)





Remarkably, if we assume the axiom of Foundation, we reach all sets this way.







Theorem 3 
For every set \(x\) there exists an ordinal \({}\alpha\) with \(x \in V_\alpha\), that is, \[
    \mathop{\mathrm{V}}= \bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} V_\alpha
\]











Remark 1. Recall that the notation \(\bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} \dots\) is really just a shortcut for the class obtained as \(\{ x \colon \exists \alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\dots\}\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(C\) be the class of all sets not in any \(V_\alpha\). Since \(\in\) is well-founded, if \(C\) is non-empty, it has a \(\in\)-minimal element \(x\). This implies that for all \(z \in x\), \(z \in \bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} V_\alpha\). Define a function \(h\) by mapping each \(z\in x\) to the least \({}\alpha\) so that \(z \in V_\alpha\). Since \(x\) is a set, \(h[x]\) is a set of ordinals, by Replacement. This set of ordinals has a supremum, say \({}\gamma\). Then \(x \subseteq V_\gamma\) and therefore,
\[
x \in \mathcal{P}(V_\gamma) = V_{\gamma+1}.
\]
Hence \(C\) must be empty, and the theorem follows.











Definition 2 For any set \(x\) we define its rank as \[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \text{ least } \alpha \text{ with } x \in V_{\alpha+1}.
\]











Exercise 1 Show that \[
\operatorname{rank}(x) = \sup\{ \operatorname{rank}(y)+1 \colon y \in x \}.
\]




We can split the question of “how large” \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) is into two sub-questions:

How “long” is \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), that is, how many ordinals are there? Axioms for large cardinals attempt to extend this “length” as far as possible.
How “wide” is \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), that is, how large is the power set of a set? A rather “slim” universe is given by the constructible sets, which we will encounter soon.

title: Induction and Recursion
text:
While the class \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\) of all ordinals is not a set, it is still transitive and well-ordered by \(\in\). Regarding the associated order \(\leq\), every set of ordinals \(a\) has a supremum \(\bigcup a = \bigcup_{\xi \in a} \xi\) and (if \(a \ne \emptyset\)) an infimum \(\bigcap a = \bigcap_{\xi \in a} \xi\), which is the smallest element of \(a\). Such a smallest element exists actually for every (non-empty) class \(A\) (since if \(\xi \in A\), we only need to find the infimum of the set of ordinals \(\le \xi\).) This allows us to prove properties about all ordinals by induction.







Proposition 1 (Induction for ordinals, I) 
For every property \(\varphi\), \[\begin{equation*}
    \forall \alpha \; [ \forall \xi < \alpha \; \varphi(\xi) \to \varphi(\alpha)] \to \forall \alpha \, \varphi(\alpha).
\end{equation*}\]




We have repeatedly used induction already for ordinals \(< \omega_1\), the first uncountable ordinal.
To prove this principle simply observe that if \(\forall \alpha \, \varphi(\alpha)\) failed there would have to be a smallest \({}\alpha\) with \(\neg \varphi(\alpha)\), contradicting the induction hypothesis.
Since every ordinal is either \(0\), a successor, or a limit ordinal, we have the following variant of induction.







Proposition 2 (Induction for ordinals, II) 
For every property \({}\varphi\), if

(i) \(\varphi(0)\),
(ii) \(\forall \alpha (\varphi(\alpha) \to \varphi(\alpha+1))\), and
(iii) \((\forall \xi < \lambda \; \varphi(\xi)) \to \varphi(\lambda))\) for all limit \(\lambda\),

then \(\forall \alpha \;  \varphi(\alpha)\).




(i) and (ii) coincide with the usual induction scheme for natural numbers. To cover all ordinals we need to add (iii).

title: Induction and Recursion
text:
The induction principle can be used to define functions by recursion. For example, addition on the natural numbers is given by
\[\begin{align*}
    x+0 \quad & =  x\\
    x+ (y+1) & =  (x + y)+1.
\end{align*}\]
In the case of ordinals, we have to consider the limit case, too.







Theorem 1 (Recursion on ordinals) 
If \(G : \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) is a function, then there exists a unique function \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that for all \(\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\),
\[
F(\alpha) = G(F\mid_{\alpha})
\]










NoteProof






Proof. The uniqueness of the function \(F\) follows by induction.
To show the existence of \(F\), we define the following:

Call \(h\) tame if \[\begin{equation*}
\exists \alpha \, (h: \alpha \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\wedge \forall \xi \in \alpha \; h(\xi) = G(h \mid_{\xi}))
\end{equation*}\]
Say \(h\) is compatible with \(g\) if \[\begin{equation*}
  \forall x \in \operatorname{Dom}(h) \cap \operatorname{Dom}(g) \; h(x) = g(x)
\end{equation*}\]

It follows by induction that any two tame functions are compatible.
This lets us define the desired \(F\) as
\[
F := \bigcup \{h \colon h\, \text{ tame}\}
\]
Then \(F\) is a function (otherwise there would be two incompatible tame functions), its domain is transitive, and satisfies the recursion condition (since it is the union of tame functions).
It remains to show that \(F\) is defined on all of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\). If \(D = \operatorname{Dom}(F) \neq \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\), then we would have \(D = \alpha\) for some ordinal \({}\alpha\). In particular \(D\) is a set therefore \(F = f\) is a set, for some tame \(f\). This \(f\) could be extended to a tame \(h = f \cup \{(\alpha,G(f \mid_{\alpha}))\}\), contradiction.




Note that we defined \(F\) explicitly as a union of all partial solutions to the recursion equation. (Of course, since \(F\) is a proper class, one has the translate the informal definition of \(F\) above into a formal expression.)
As with induction, we have the following variant of the recursion principle.







Proposition 3 (Recursion on ordinals, variant) 
If \(G, H: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) are functions and \(a\) is a set, then there exists a unique function \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{align*}
    F(0) \quad & =  a\\
    F(\alpha+1) & =  G(\alpha,F(\alpha)) \\    
    F(\lambda) \quad & =  H(\lambda, \{F(\xi) \colon \xi<\lambda \}) \quad \text{for } \operatorname{Lim}(\lambda).
\end{align*}\]




We can establish a similar principle for a well-ordering \(<\) on a class \(A\). In case of a proper class, though, we have to require that for every \(a \in A\), the class of all predecessors of \(a\) \[\begin{equation*}
S(a,<): = \{x \in A\colon x < a \},
\end{equation*}\] is a set (if \(A\) is a set, this follows automatically by Separation). If this is the case, the recursion principle yields a function \(F: A \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    F(a) = G(a,F\mid_{S(a,<)}).
\end{equation*}\]

title: Induction and Recursion
text:
More generally, we can define induction and recursion on well-founded relations. We already encountered those in a previous chapter.







Definition 1 
A relation \(R\) on a class \(A\) is well-founded if it satisfies the minimality condition \[\begin{equation*}
    (\operatorname{Min}_R) \qquad  \emptyset \neq b \subset A \to \exists x \in b \; \forall y \in b \, (  \neg y R x)
\end{equation*}\] and the set condition \[\begin{equation*}
    \forall x \in A \; S(a,R):= \{x \colon x R a\} \text{ is a set}
\end{equation*}\]




If \(A\) is a set, the minimality condition is again automatically satisfied by Separation.
The set condition allows for taking the \(R\)-transitive closure of a set \(a \in A\): the smallest superset \(\operatorname{TC}_R(a)\) of \(a\) that is \(R\)-transitive:
\[ \forall x \in \operatorname{TC}_R(a)\; S(x,R) \subseteq  \operatorname{TC}_R(a)\]
This is done by recursion over the natural numbers. The following is an important example.







Example 1 (Transitive closure of a set) 
By the axiom of Foundation, \(\in\) is a well-founded relation on \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\). (The set condition is satisfied since \(S(a,\in)=a\).)
We can form the transitive closure, the smallest transitive superset, of a set \(a\) as
\[\begin{align*}
    \operatorname{TC}(a):&= a \cup \bigcup a \cup \bigcup \bigcup a \ldots
= \bigcup_{n< \omega} U^n(a), \quad \text{ where} \\
&U^0(a) = a, U^{n+1}(a) = \bigcup U^n(a).
\end{align*}\]
This is an example of definition by recursion along \(\mathbb{N}\).




We can use the existence of \(\operatorname{TC}_R\) as a set to strengthen the minimality condition to subclasses, similar to the case of the well-ordering of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\):







Lemma 1 
For every non-empty class \(B \subseteq A\), there exists \(x \in B\) such that
\[
    \forall y \in B \;  \neg y R x
\]




To prove this lemma, simply pick any \(x \in B\), take its transitive \(R\)-closure, and intersect it with \(B\):
\[
    C = \operatorname{TC}_R(x) \cap B.
\]
\(C\) is a set, and by the minimality condition \((\operatorname{Min}_R)\) has an \(R\)-minimal element \(a\). \(a\) has to be minimal for \(B\), too, since otherwise there exists \(b \in B\) with \(b R a\). Since \(a \in \operatorname{TC}_R(x)\), \(b \in \operatorname{TC}_R(x)\), and therefore \(b \in C\), contradicting the minimality of \(a\).
The lemma implies a corresponding induction principle for well-founded relations:
\[\begin{equation*}
    (\operatorname{Ind}_R) \qquad  \forall x \in A [ \forall y ( yRx \, \to \varphi(y)) \to \varphi(x)] \to \forall x \in A \, \varphi(x)).
\end{equation*}\]
This in turn yields the following.







Theorem 2 (Recursion principle for well-founded relations) 
Let \(R\) be a well-founded relation on a class \(A\). For every function \(G : A \times \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) there exists a unique function \(F: A \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    F(a) = G(a,F \mid_{\{x \mid xRa\}})  \text{ for all } a \in A.
\end{equation*}\]

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Where We’re Going

This course compares three modern foundations of mathematics: set theory, category theory, type theory
Before any of that: a 19th-century story about rigor, completeness, and infinity
Today: Prologue – Bolzano (1817) \(\to\) Dedekind (1872) \(\to\) Cantor (1874)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
section: Gauss and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
text:
Gauss and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra

THM: Every non-constant polynomial has a root over the complex numbers.
Gauss’s proofs (from 1799 on) quietly depend on the Intermediate Value Theorem

\[
f \text{ continuous},\ f(a)<0,\ f(b)>0 \ \implies\ f(c)=0 \text{ for some } c\in(a,b)
\]

IVT feels obvious: a curve can’t get from below the axis to above it without crossing. (Gauss and many others at the time thought so.)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Bolzano’s Insight (1817)


Bernard Bolzano was the first to realize importance of continuity in the proof of Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

He attempted a genuine proof of the IVT.
But he had no clear concept of the real numbers to work with.
His proof was not fully satisfactory — a rigorous treatment of continuity had to wait for Weierstrass (1874).








Bernard Bolzano
(1781–1848)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Completeness: An Ancient Intuition
Bolzano’s realization:
\[
\text{completeness of } \mathbb{R} \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \text{absence of gaps}
\]

Ancient intuition: a line has no gaps
But then — what are the “parts” of a line?

To capture this, Bolzano introduced two principles:

the least upper bound principle
the nested interval property
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
How to Prove Completeness?

Bolzano could state completeness — but not prove it
Proving it requires first knowing what a real number is
That formalization of \(\mathbb{R}\) did not arrive until the 1870s

e.g. via Dedekind cuts
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Dedekind’s Breakthrough (1872)


Dedekind’s key move: stop presupposing what \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) is.

A real number is a Dedekind cut \((L, U)\).


\((L,U)\) partitions \(\mathbb{Q}\): every element of \(L\) is less than every element of \(U\)
Completeness is now straightforward — union of left-sides of cuts defines a cut.








Richard Dedekind
(1831–1916)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
A Deeper Problem
Dedekind (1872) solved the problem “What is a real number?”
— but in doing so, he opened a deeper problem: the nature of infinity.

Reals are introduced as (pairs of) infinite sets of rationals
There seemed to be no way around this
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
A New Kind of Object

Sets — and infinity — stop being background intuition.
They become mathematical objects in their own right
This shift is the seed of everything that follows in this course
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Cantor (1874): Two Kinds of Infinity


Cantor showed that \(\mathbb{N}\) and \(\mathbb{R}\) represent different types of infinity.
His first proof of the uncountability of \(\mathbb{R}\):

Take any sequence \((x_m)_{m \in \mathbb{N}}\) of distinct real numbers.
Construct nested intervals that exclude one \(x_m\) at a time.








Georg Cantor
(1845–1918)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Cantor’s Construction
Build nested intervals
\[
a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < b_2 < b_1 < b_0
\]
such that
\[
\forall m\ \exists i \quad x_m \notin [a_i, b_i]
\]
(at each stage, shrink the interval just enough to exclude the next \(x_m\))
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Cantor’s Argument
By the nested interval property:
\[
\bigcap_i [a_i, b_i] \neq \emptyset
\]
Let \(x\) be a point in this intersection.

By construction, \(x \neq x_i\) for every \(i\).
So \((x_m)\) could not have enumerated all of \(\mathbb{R}\).
Hence \(\mathbb{R}\) is uncountable.


This only works because \(\mathbb{R}\) is complete — the nested interval property fails over \(\mathbb{Q}\).
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
A Bonus: Transcendental Numbers
The same construction gives more than uncountability:

The set of algebraic numbers is countable.
So the same nested-interval argument produces a real number not among the algebraic numbers

\[
\implies \text{transcendental numbers exist}
\]
— without ever exhibiting one!
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Not Everyone Was Convinced
Dedekind’s cuts and ideals, Cantor’s infinite sets — both rely on purely existential proofs:

they show an object exists, without showing how to construct or compute it.
this was a genuinely new style of mathematics in the 1870s–80s.

Not everyone welcomed it.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Kronecker’s Critique








Leopold Kronecker
(1823–1891)


Leopold Kronecker, one of the leading algebraists of the day, objected on principle.

1870: points out that the accumulation point in the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem cannot be constructed by elementary operations from the rational numbers.
1882: publicly attacked Dedekind’s ideals — used to prove unique factorization exists but the proof does not tell you how to compute it.
Combated Cantor’s transfinite sets as well.


“Die ganzen Zahlen hat der liebe Gott gemacht, alles andere ist Menschenwerk.” — attributed to Kronecker: “God made the integers; all else is the work of man.”
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
A Debate Ensues

Dedekind replied in 1888 with a fully set-theoretic theory of the natural numbers (“Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen?”, includes his definition of an infinite set).
The “early round” of the debate ended in victory for the infinitary side.

Hurwitz, Minkowski, Hilbert, Volterra, Peano, Hadamard, Klein all sided with Dedekind and Cantor.

Arbitrary functions, infinite sets, and existential proofs become the mainstream of analysis and algebra.

Kronecker’s constructivist objection doesn’t disappear — it resurfaces in Brouwer’s intuitionism, decades later.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Frege’s Logicism


Gottlob Frege pursued an even more ambitious foundation: reduce all of arithmetic to pure logic.

Basic mathematical concepts should be definable in purely logical terms
Basic mathematical truths should be derivable from purely logical laws
Central logical law (the comprehension principle): for any well-defined property \(p\), there is a set \[
\{x : p(x)\}
\]
Frege built his Grundgesetze der Arithmetik (1893, 1903) on exactly this idea.








Gottlob Frege
(1848–1925)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Frege’s Logicism
Frege needed the comprehension principle to define the natural numbers in a purely logical way.

Frege (as later Russell and Whitehead) realized that natural numbers are logical attributes that belong to concepts, not to things.
“There are four horses in the barn” should be thought of as four objects fall under the concept “horse in barn”.
If \(f\) is a concept, we can then define “at least two objects fall under \(f\)” as \[
2_m(f) := \exists x \exists y \: [ x \neq y \: \wedge f(x) \: \wedge \: f(y)]
\] and can define the number \(2\) as \(2() := 2_m() \: \wedge \ \neg 3_m()\).

For this definition to work, Frege needed the comprehension principle - every concept determines a class containing exactly the objects falling under it.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Russell’s Paradox (1901–02)
Around 1901, Bertrand Russell (and, independently, Zermelo) found that comprehension is inconsistent.
Let \[
R = \{\, x : x \notin x \,\}
\]

If \(R \in R\), then by definition \(R \notin R\)
If \(R \notin R\), then by definition \(R \in R\)

Either way, contradiction. The very principle underlying Frege’s logic — and “naive” set theory generally — collapses.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Letter to Frege, 16 June 1902



“Let \(w\) be the predicate: to be a predicate that cannot be predicated of itself. Can \(w\) be predicated of itself? From each answer its opposite follows. […] Likewise there is no class (as a totality) of those classes which, each taken as a totality, do not belong to themselves.”
— Bertrand Russell, letter to Gottlob Frege








Bertrand Russell
(1872–1970)


Russell had been reading Frege’s Grundgesetze closely — and found the one crack in its foundation.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Frege’s Reply, 22 June 1902

“Your discovery of the contradiction caused me the greatest surprise and, I would almost say, consternation, since it has shaken the basis on which I intended to build arithmetic. […] It is all the more serious since, with the loss of my Rule V, not only the foundations of my arithmetic, but also the sole possible foundations of arithmetic, seem to vanish.”
— Gottlob Frege, letter to Bertrand Russell

Frege added a hasty appendix to Volume II of the Grundgesetze, already at the printer, acknowledging the disaster.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
What now?
Other set theoretic paradoxes had emerged before Russell’s.

Burali-Forti paradox (Cantor, 1896): There cannot be a set of all ordinals.

But these were tied deeply to Cantor’s transfinite set theory, which many people still viewed as remote and suspect.
Russell’s antinomy struck right at the heart of the very foundation of all of mathematics: the efforts to define the natural numbers.
